event.family_civilian_02_scarcity_fallba: A button comes off your coat again. The person housing you takes out an almost empty spool and explains that a new garment must wait; this one has to last at least until the next market.
You hold the spool while the adult threads the needle again. They tell you not to move so the last length is not lost.
You point to the button under the chair. The adult picks it up and decides to reuse it instead of looking for new cloth.
Cover the hole with your hand
You press your hand over the hole in the coat. The adult laughs, then sees one button will not be enough if the seam gives again.
Keep the spool safe like the flour
You move the spool away from the edge and any damp, like the sacks saved under the leak. The adult notices you protect what cannot easily be replaced first.
The thread breaks on the first knot. There is just enough left to try once more, not enough to reinforce the whole seam.
You hold the cloth taut while the adult ties the knot again. The last thread is enough for the button, not to reinforce the rest.
You stop the adult from using the last few inches on a hidden seam. They save it for the next urgent tear.
You take off the coat and refuse to stand by the needle. The adult finishes the stitching alone before giving it back.
event.family_civilian_02_enterprise_fall: The Parcel That Will Not Fit
An oversized delivery blocks the entrance to the family workplace. The courier refuses to unpack in the street; inside, no one wants to move the goods already stored.
You duck under the corner of the crate sticking through the doorway. The courier immediately sees where it actually catches.
Point to the space by the wall
You point to a gap behind a smaller stack. An employee checks whether moving a few boxes would clear the angle.
You push a small box out of the way. The adults stop you before the big stack, but realize a corner of floor has opened up.
Point out the small storeroom behind the crate
You point to the door you remember from the old keyring. An employee immediately checks whether that storeroom can take the smaller boxes.
The courier measures the doorway again and taps the crate. It is only a hand’s width too wide to pass without taking everything apart.
You keep the measuring cord taut to the wall while the courier turns the crate. He finds the missing angle without emptying the whole shop.
You carry only the light boxes to the pavement. The adults move the heavy load and keep the task at your scale.
You sit against the wall and leave the adults to solve their delivery. They stop asking you where to move goods too heavy for you.
The delivery cart loses a wheel in front of your home. The courier knows your family and asks you to keep three parcels dry while he looks for a repairer.
You take the smallest parcel and put it under cover. The courier thanks you before stacking the other two himself.
You recognize the painted mark on one parcel and point it out. The neighbor across the street immediately starts asking for his.
You hold the door with your foot while the courier slides the parcels inside. The neighbor can clearly see where his order has been stored.
Keep the parcel away from the puddle
You move the marked parcel away from the water without being asked. The courier realizes shelter has to be organized before distribution.
event.family_civilian_02_local_fallback_: The courier stacks the parcels just under cover. One bears a neighbor’s mark, and that neighbor is already asking for the order from across the street.
Carry the parcel to the neighbor
You carry the marked parcel to the neighbor in front of the courier. The favor is simple and no one can claim another parcel was delivered.
Keep the other two behind the door
You shut the door on the two remaining parcels. The neighbor gets his without turning your entryway into a depot for the whole street.
You call after the courier instead of handing parcels out yourself. He comes back to manage the delivery he left with your family too quickly.
event.family_civilian_03_child_runs_coun: At seven, an adult lets you mind the counter while they fetch a crate downstairs. A customer pushes a complicated order toward you and says he is already late.
Keep the Berrys on the counter
You keep your hand in front of the coins instead of taking them. The customer realizes he will have to wait for the adult to finish his order.
You call the adult's name down toward the storeroom. The customer sighs but stops talking to you as if you already ran the shop.
You copy the three requested items onto a scrap of paper without touching the money. The adult can decide the rest when they return.
You keep the Berrys separate until a clear line is written, like your father did after the payment dispute. The customer stops pressing you.
The customer sets down his Berrys and begins listing what he wants. The adult is still downstairs; answering now means making a real decision for the household.
You gather only the items you can identify safely and leave the complicated price to the adult. The customer leaves a little later, but with the right order.
Move the Berrys out of reach
You slide the coins behind the counter and wait. The customer can no longer pressure you by waving money under your nose.
You close the small counter gate until the adult returns. The customer complains, but no one can turn your help into full responsibility.
event.family_civilian_03_school_or_shift: An exercise book sticks out beneath your apron when a new order arrives. The teacher expects the work tomorrow; the household needs another pair of hands until closing.
Finish the line in the workbook
You finish the line you started before closing the workbook. The adult can clearly see what they are asking you to interrupt for the order.
Ask how late you are needed
You ask whether the help means ten minutes or until closing. No one can answer with just 'a little' anymore.
Lay the apron over the workbook
You place the apron over the workbook without putting it on. The gesture leaves both obligations visible before you choose one.
Clear space for the workbook like a plate
You push the tools just far enough to make a real place for the workbook, repeating the boundary set at the table years earlier. The adult understands before you answer.
The notebook stays open by the till while work piles up. Finishing one before night means leaving the other to someone else.
Work one hour, then reopen the book
You help until the next bell, then reopen your workbook in front of everyone. The household gets your help without swallowing the whole evening.
Finish the homework before the till
You finish your homework while an adult takes the first order. Only then do you put on the apron.
Give back the apron without closing the book
You hand the apron back and keep the workbook open. The adults have to find another pair of hands for this order.
event.family_civilian_03_neighbor_debt_c: The Screwdriver That Never Came Back
The neighbor who still owes a sack of flour comes to borrow the household’s only good screwdriver. He promises to return it tonight; tomorrow morning, a paid repair depends on that exact tool.
Hold the screwdriver behind your back
You hide the screwdriver behind your back while the neighbor promises 'tonight' again. He has to speak to your family instead of only to you.
You point to the broken piece already waiting on the bench. The neighbor finally sees what the tool he wants is needed for.
You offer the bent old screwdriver instead of the good one. He can patch his shutter without taking the tool needed for the paid repair.
Mark the return time in chalk
You mark the promised return time on the doorframe like a debt that can be checked. The neighbor laughs less once the deadline is visible.
The neighbor keeps his hand out. Behind him, his own shutter hangs crooked; at home, tomorrow’s repair is already written in the order book.
Lend the good one until sunset
You mark the return time in the book and give him the good screwdriver. If he is late, everyone will know tomorrow's repair is at risk.
You give him the old screwdriver and keep the good one in the shop. The favor is real without sacrificing tomorrow's job.
You put both screwdrivers back in the drawer and close it. The neighbor leaves to find another solution instead of adding a debt to the old one.
event.family_civilian_03_orphan_receipt_: The woman housing you finds three receipts for your meals in different pockets. She wants to know who pays what before keeping you another month; no one has kept the account properly.
You sort the receipts by paper color and recognize which adults wrote them. The woman hosting you can finally call each person by name.
Write your name on the box
You write your name on the empty box. The adult realizes the papers deciding where you live cannot keep being scattered.
Put all three receipts in the box
You put all three receipts together without deciding who is right. The box becomes at least one place the adults will all have to look.
Ask for one paper per night
You tie each receipt to a night someone actually housed you. Your host stops counting indistinct favors.
She empties the receipts onto the table and adds an empty box. If the adults cannot agree, your next lodging will be decided before dinner.
Carry the box to all three adults
You carry the box to all three adults and each adds what they remember paying. Your host finally gets a clear enough account to keep you for the month.
Ask for one receipt per week
You ask for one paper per week kept in the box. The adults agree to a rule simple enough for you to check yourself.
Push the receipts back to the adults
You push the papers back toward the adults who created them. They have to settle their accounts without making you the accountant of your own housing.
event.family_civilian_03_employees_know_: An employee stops you before you put the wage envelopes on the wrong desk. He shows you the names and overtime notes on the back: every envelope belongs to someone you see each day.
You read the names aloud one by one while rebuilding the stack. The employees correct two mistakes and the argument stops being only about abstract numbers.
Bring the light envelope to its owner
You bring the lighter envelope to its owner instead of hiding it in the stack. They immediately ask why Berrys are missing.
Keep the light envelope on top
You put it on top of the pile so it cannot disappear. The adult signing wages has to deal with it before moving on.
Hand out only the complete envelopes
You set the light envelope aside instead of burying it in the stack. The adults have to fix that one before you resume handing them out.
The employee makes you rebuild the stack in the right order. One envelope is lighter than last week and its owner is already waiting in the corridor.
You count the overtime marks with the employee and find a missed line. The adult corrects the envelope in front of both of you.
You call in the person concerned before anyone decides for them. The difference is explained aloud instead of vanishing into the books.
Return the whole stack to the manager
You return the envelopes without agreeing to hand them out. The adults have to own the wage differences they created.
event.family_civilian_03_giant_delivery_: A heavy crate must cross an alley too narrow for you to carry it normally. The workers want to roll it; the workshop manager thinks the route can be changed without blocking the whole neighborhood.
Turn the crate without lifting it
You try turning the crate on the ground. It touches the wall before the corner, showing exactly where the alley is too narrow.
Ask the stalls to move back one step
You ask the two neighbors whose stalls stick out most. They agree to move back a little if the crate goes through in one pass.
You mark the crate's width and turn in chalk on the ground. The workers see they can move two stalls instead of the whole street.
Measure with the old bench rope
You reuse the rope once used to adapt the workshop and mark the crate's width through the corner. The workers stop guessing by eye.
The workers set the crate on two rollers and neighbors already start moving their stalls. One bad maneuver will close the alley for everyone.
Guide the rollers through the turn
You reposition the rollers as the crate turns and call out when it nears the wall. The delivery gets through without closing the whole alley.
Clear the children from the alley
You refuse to start while younger children are still playing near the rollers. The neighbors clear the alley before the crate moves.
Make the crate wait for a quieter hour
You ask to leave the crate at the start until the stalls close. The workers complain, but the neighborhood is not treated as an obstacle to bulldoze through.
event.family_civilian_03_fishman_backroo: At seven, a neighboring merchant offers you occasional work, then hands you an apron meant for the back room. He claims some customers are “not ready” to see a Fish-Man at the counter.
Hang the apron on the counter side
You take the apron and hang it in front of the curtain where customers can see it. The merchant has to explain why he wanted it behind.
Ask for the same job as the other child
You point to the other shop helper and ask why your jobs would be different. The merchant can no longer hide behind 'difficult customers.'
Leave the apron on the counter
You leave it there. The pay remains tempting, but the merchant has to decide whether he actually wants your help or only wants you hidden.
Route the offer through your mother
You take the apron and wage offer to your mother before answering. The merchant realizes he cannot isolate you to impose his rule.
The merchant hangs the apron on a nail behind the curtain. The wage is fair; only the place he assigns you is the problem.
You accept the tasks but keep the curtain open. The merchant protests, then lets the first customer see you doing the same work as everyone else.
Demand the counter for the same tasks
You agree to help only if counter duties remain open to you. The merchant has to choose between your work and his discriminatory rule.
Give the apron back to the merchant
You hand the apron back without stepping behind the curtain. The pay disappears with the offer, but your place in the street does not.
event.family_civilian_03_work_fallback.t: The shutter is already half lowered when a neighbor arrives with a broken item he needs tomorrow. The household promised an evening without work; the repair would still take less than an hour.
event.family_civilian_03_work_fallback.c: Inspect the break under the lamp
You inspect the break under the lamp and say it is not as simple as it looks. The neighbor stops insisting it will 'only take ten minutes.'
Carry the item to the adult
You carry the broken item to the adult closing the shop. They can see the problem without fully reopening the counter.
Set the item beside the plate
You place the repair beside the meal so it will not be forgotten tomorrow. The neighbor leaves without turning the evening into another hour of work.
event.family_civilian_03_work_fallback_i: The neighbor sets the item on the counter without pressing. Behind you, the plates are already served and someone calls that dinner is getting cold.
You take apart the two simple pieces while the adult handles the delicate part. The repair moves forward without swallowing the whole evening.
You tie a note to the repair and sit back down. The neighbor gets a guaranteed place tomorrow, not a family that cancels dinner.
You give the item back and tell the neighbor to return at opening. Dinner stays dinner even if the customer is unhappy.
event.family_civilian_03_care_fallback.t: A distant relative arrives with an injured leg and asks for only one night. There is no free bed; someone will have to sleep in a chair or find another door for him.
event.family_civilian_03_care_fallback.c: Bring the blanket to the chair
You put the dry blanket on the chair before the adults finish arguing. The traveler understands they can at least rest tonight.
Ask the neighbor if they have a bed
You go next door to ask whether they have a bed. The answer turns the welcome into a concrete problem instead of an endless debate.
You put your things on your bed before anyone volunteers it. The adults have to find a solution that does not automatically displace the child.
event.family_civilian_03_care_fallback_i: A Bed That Does Not Exist
The traveler is already sitting by the entrance. A dry blanket hangs over the back of the only chair wide enough to sleep in.
Make the chair ready for the night
You bring a cushion, water, and the blanket. The traveler sleeps sitting up for one night without turning your bed into the family's default spare resource.
You return with a bed next door for tonight. The traveler stays nearby without squeezing the household until someone else is displaced.
Leave the hosting to the adults
You refuse to give up your place or carry the problem. The adults figure out where the traveler will sleep themselves.
A merchant finally returns the household’s large borrowed basket, but one handle is broken. The morning delivery depends on it, and he offers to pay later rather than repair it now.
You lift the basket by the handle and it gives way immediately. The merchant stops claiming it will 'hold tomorrow.'
Point to the empty delivery spot
You point to where the basket should be ready for tomorrow morning. The merchant sees his delay is already affecting another job.
Put his two coins on the handle
You put his two small coins on the broken wood. Even at seven, the gap between the repair and his offer becomes obvious.
event.family_civilian_03_trade_fallback_: The merchant sets two small coins on the broken basket. They will not cover a new handle, but refusing means reopening an old favor.
Take the coins and repair it together
You take his coins on condition he helps fix the handle now. The basket will be ready tomorrow and the old favor stops dragging on.
Keep the basket until it is fully repaired
You keep the basket at home and ask him to return with enough to cover the rest. Tomorrow's delivery is delayed, but the debt does not grow.
You give his money back and ask for a repaired basket, not another promise. He leaves carrying the problem he caused.
event.family_civilian_04_apprenticeship_: At ten, a craftsperson from another district brings an apprenticeship letter. They want you three days a week; the household would lose your help on those days, but you would learn a trade outside the family.
You read the three days listed in the letter and compare them with the days the household relies on you most. The conflict becomes concrete.
You ask to see the workshop before promising three days a week. The artisan agrees to a short visit instead of demanding a blind answer.
Fold the letter into your workbook
You tuck the letter into your workbook instead of answering in front of everyone. The household has to give you at least until tonight.
You place on the letter the workbook you refused to abandon at seven. The artisan understands the apprenticeship will also have to leave room for school.
The letter stays open between your notebook and the order book. The craftsperson wants an answer before offering the place to another child.
You offer two trial days before accepting the full schedule. The artisan holds the place and the household can see what your absence actually changes.
Keep one fixed day for the household
You accept the apprenticeship while keeping one fixed day for home. No one gets everything they wanted, but the schedule can work.
Turn down the place this year
You return the letter without insulting the offer. The artisan gives the place to someone else and the household knows the choice has a real cost.
event.family_civilian_04_landlord_deadli: The landlord circles a date in red in his ledger: after that day, he takes back the rear room. The household can pay part of it, sell equipment, or ask for more time.
Measure what fits in the room
You measure the bed, crates, and the most profitable tool against the walls. Selling things or losing the room stops being abstract.
You ask the landlord exactly how much is overdue, not how much he would like. He has to give a number before talking about taking the room back.
Mark the date on the wall
You copy the red date onto the wall by the door. The whole household can now see how many days remain before the room is taken.
Refuse to pay with another favor
You recall the old chain of favors and repairs that never quite settled. The household drops the idea of adding another vague favor to the rent.
Keep One Room of the Home
The ledger remains open on the table. Behind the landlord, the threatened room holds a bed, crates, and the household’s most profitable tool.
You identify the crates no longer in use and the household sells them first. It does not cover everything, but it protects the tool that earns money.
Keep the tool and negotiate the room
You show the landlord that removing the tool would make payment even harder. He agrees to a shorter extension rather than destroying the income source.
You stop the household from promising a date it knows it cannot meet. The landlord leaves without an easy guarantee, but no one adds a lie to the debt.
event.family_civilian_04_orphan_signatur: A school accepts your late enrollment, but the form requires the signature of a stable guardian. Three adults have housed you this year; at first none agrees to be the one the administration will call afterward.
Take the form to your latest host
You take the form to the adult hosting you this week. They can no longer leave the signature as an abstract problem for the other two.
Ask what the signature commits to
You ask the secretary what the signer would actually be responsible for. He explains calls, absences, and obligations instead of merely pointing at the blank line.
Write all three names in the margin
You write the names of all three adults who hosted you this year. The secretary finally sees the problem is not a total lack of help, but the lack of one sole guardian.
You put down the box that has tracked your housing for years. The secretary sees real responsibilities even if they do not fit under one name.
The clerk pushes the form to the edge of the desk. Without a signature today, the place goes back to the waiting list tomorrow.
The adult hosting you signs for the school year after the secretary limits the obligation. You get the place without pretending they become your parent.
Attach notes from the other two
You get one main signature and two notes confirming who can be called as backup. The school has a responsible adult without erasing your real network.
You refuse to let an adult sign while pretending to be something they are not. The secretary keeps your file open while looking for an honest administrative solution.
event.family_civilian_04_business_expans: The Plan Drawn for the Second Shop

In the family business office, the managers unroll plans for a second shop. Your name is already written on a future floor, while employees wait to learn who will run the first counter during the expansion.
Erase your name from the future office
You erase your name from the small room and ask why it was already reserved for you. The adults have to separate the expansion from your future.
Ask who will run the first counter
You point to the main counter with no name beside it. An employee answers before the managers and reveals where the plan actually lacks someone.
Change the office into shared storage
You redraw 'your office' as shared storage. The adults realize the plan can change before assigning you a role.
Put the corrected envelope on the plan
You place an old corrected wage envelope over the room drawn in your name. The managers remember expansion means little if the first shop loses its people.
The Office Already Has Your Name
On the second-shop plan, a small room has your name penciled in. An employee points to the current shop counter: nobody has yet been named to stay there during construction.
You suggest keeping the room flexible until a real need appears. The expansion moves forward without writing your job ten years in advance.
You ask that the first shop keep enough staff before the second opens. The employees get a transition plan instead of a vague promise.
Refuse any room in your name
You refuse to have any room reserved for you before you have chosen a trade. The adults can expand the business, not decide your place inside it.
event.family_civilian_04_giant_public_de: An important delivery must cross the market at its busiest hour. Your size lets you carry the load above the stalls, but a fall would cause more damage than an ordinary cart.
You lift the load just enough to feel its balance without moving. The straps pull to one side and the merchants see the risk before the start.
Ask to clear the low awnings
You ask the three most exposed merchants to raise their awnings. They agree if the crossing happens in one attempt.
Mark a path on the ground
You mark in chalk where your feet will go. The vendors move only what actually intrudes into that lane.
You reuse the rollers-and-markings method instead of relying only on your strength. The merchants take part in the passage instead of merely enduring it.
The merchants clear a narrow line between their awnings. The load is strapped; the remaining question is whether you carry it through or wait until closing.
You move only when each merchant confirms their stall is clear. The load crosses above the crowd without turning the market into a spectacle forced on everyone.
Wait for the square to clear
You refuse to carry above a packed crowd. The delivery is late, but it crosses after most customers have left.
You refuse to let your size automatically replace safe transport. The adults reorganize the delivery with the cart and several porters.
event.family_civilian_04_fishman_counter: A trader offers the household a regular contract, then adds by hand that you will work out of customers’ sight. He says it will “avoid trouble”; the person signing for the household asks why your face appears in his terms.
You circle the handwritten sentence in charcoal until it becomes the most visible part of the contract. The merchant can no longer pass it off as a detail.
You ask which specific customer demanded not to see you. The merchant cannot name one, and his excuse weakens.
Push the pen away from the contract
You push the pen away from the signature line. The household gets time to answer before one merchant's habit becomes a written rule.
Lay the old apron over the clause
You lay the old apron once meant to hide you over the sentence trying to do the same thing again. The merchant sees exactly what history he is repeating.
The trader taps the added clause and promises the same price. The contract stays open in front of you so you can answer before it is signed.
You cross out the sentence and return the contract. The merchant accepts the same price without the restriction because he genuinely wants the goods.
You ask for the contract to state that roles do not depend on Race. The merchant signs under a rule opposite to the one he tried to impose.
You tear the page before the household can sign. The large contract disappears, but the humiliating condition does not enter your working rules.
event.family_civilian_04_neighborhood_di: Two neighbors argue outside the shop over a broken tool and name your family as witness. Customers slow down to listen; answering could settle it or tie your household name to their quarrel.
You inspect where the tool broke before listening to either story. An old visible crack makes at least one accusation less convincing.
You ask each neighbor to describe the loan without the other interrupting. The customers hear two stories that do not match.
Take the tool inside the shop
You take the tool out of the street. The argument continues, but no one can wave it at customers as evidence.
You find on the tool the mark added after the screwdriver that did not come back. The neighbors have to compare their memories with a real trace.
One neighbor sets the broken tool on the sill; the other demands that you confirm who had it last. The whole street is listening now.
You recount only the moment you actually saw and refuse to fill in the rest. The neighbors have to settle the unknown part without using your name as a verdict.
Get the tool repaired before the argument
You propose each pays part of the repair now and argues about blame later. The tool stops being unusable while they fight.
Take your family’s name out of it
You say your family will not witness what it did not see. The neighbors leave carrying their dispute instead of dropping it at the shop.
event.family_civilian_04_work_family_fal: Dinner starts without the adult who is still closing the workplace. An urgent order pushed closing back; someone suggests carrying a plate there instead of waiting any longer.
Carry the plate to the shop
You take the wrapped plate across the street. The adult sees dinner arrive in the middle of the urgent order.
Ask the customer to wait ten minutes
You ask the customer directly whether they can wait ten minutes for a hot meal. Their answer stops the adult pretending there is no choice.
Keep the chair empty at the table
You refuse to clear the absent person's place. The empty chair stays visible until they return or accept missing dinner.
The plate is already wrapped in a cloth. Outside, the workplace light is the only one still burning in the street.
You help with the simple part so the shop can close sooner, then you return together with the plate still warm.
Close for ten minutes to eat
You turn the sign and the adult eats with the family before reopening. The customer waits, but the evening does not vanish entirely into work.
Leave the plate and go home
You leave the plate by the tool and go home without working. The adult can choose to finish, but that choice does not automatically become yours.
event.family_civilian_04_scarcity_care_f: The doctor leaves a bill after a short visit and refuses to remove the basic medicine. The household can pay in installments, offer work in exchange, or delay another expense.
You ask the doctor to separate the cost of medicine from the visit. The household can finally see which part cannot be postponed today.
Ask what service he would accept
You ask what concrete service could replace part of the payment. The doctor names a specific delivery instead of a vague debt.
Write the due dates on the bill
You write the proposed due dates directly on the bill. The household can see whether the plan is realistic before agreeing.
Treat the Illness Without Emptying the House
The bill is folded beneath the medicine box. The doctor is only waiting to know what form the payment will take.
You set aside the medicine money first and the household negotiates the rest separately. Treatment begins without pretending the whole bill disappeared.
The doctor accepts one delivery to the clinic for part of his visit. The debt becomes limited, dated, and verifiable.
You reject a schedule that would consume the next weeks of income. The doctor keeps the bill open, but the household does not sign up for its next crisis.
event.family_civilian_04_enterprise_race: The Contract Refused at the Counter
A regular customer brings a larger contract than usual, then hesitates over the terms. He wants the work, but only if the household accepts an unrealistic deadline and a lower price.
You put the lower price beside the shorter deadline. Even without running the business, you can see the customer is asking for two concessions at once.
Ask which promise is written down
You ask where the 'future orders' he promises are written. The client admits none are guaranteed on paper.
Move the pen off the price
You move the pen away from the price line and let the adults talk without a rushed signature.
A Good Customer, a Bad Contract
The customer places his pen on the price line and promises more orders later. Today, nothing guarantees that promise.
You propose keeping the price if the customer accepts a deadline the shop can actually meet. He chooses the date over an impossible discount.
Calculate the cost of late hours
You make the adults count what the deadline would cost in late hours. The customer sees his discount would be paid by workers, not an abstract margin.
You return the paper unsigned and without banking on future orders. The good customer remains a customer, but this bad contract does not become your standard.
event.family_civilian_05_workshop_inheri: At thirteen, the family places the workplace key in front of you. It is not a career promise: it only means you can return, help, learn, or lock the door behind you.
Try the key in the lock
You try the key in the workshop door. It still turns: the access is real before anyone decides what it should mean.
Ask who could take the key back
You ask whether the key stays yours when you leave or only while you help here. The family has to define access before talking about a trade.
Set the key beside the till
You set the key beside the till instead of taking it. The gesture forces the family to state what it is actually passing on.
Set the apprenticeship letter beside the key
You place the apprenticeship letter from three years ago beside the key. The family has to discuss the workshop as one access among others, not the only serious future.
The key stays between you as the last customer leaves. No one asks you to choose a profession today; only what this door will mean after you leave.
You keep access to the workshop. Along with the key, your family gives you a small toolkit so the craft can travel with you.
The family hands you the savings set aside for your first departure.
You return the key. The workshop's grey cat follows you to the door and refuses to go back to its crate.
event.family_civilian_05_household_savin: The household finally opens the small savings box hidden beneath a floorboard. It holds enough to solve one real problem, not enough to change everything: debt, departure, or emergency reserve.
Count the share that could be yours
You count only what the household could give you without emptying the box. The rest stays visible as shared security.
You ask which debt waited the longest so this box could exist. A specific name finally replaces years of 'later.'
You lower the lid without taking a coin. The household has to decide whether this reserve opens for you or for itself.
Set aside the next rent first
You set aside the next rent payment before discussing your share. The household knows exactly what it can pass on without recreating the old emergency.
The coins and small notes are counted three times. Everyone knows exactly which expenses were postponed to fill this box.
The household gives you a liquid share large enough to begin without erasing years of caution.
The merchant strikes out the oldest line in front of you. The debt leaves the books and the neighborhood sees the household kept its word.
You leave the money with the household and keep the certainty that a future emergency already has an answer.
Three adults who housed you each write an address on the same sheet of paper. None claims to be your parent; they are only offering specific doors you can knock on later.
You read the three addresses and recognize what each actually offers: a bed, work, or simply someone who will answer.
You ask which of the three adults would actually answer a call for you six months from now. Each has to answer for themselves.
Fold the paper into your pocket
You fold the paper without thanking anyone too quickly. The adults understand addresses only matter if they remain true after you leave.
You add the adult who once agreed to sign for school. Their address becomes a responsibility already proven, not just another promise.
event.family_civilian_05_orphan_network_: The paper passes from hand to hand. One address offers a bed, another occasional work, the third only someone who will answer a letter.
You keep an imperfect but real network of people who accepted concrete obligations.
You reduce the network to one reliable person future employers or landlords can contact.
You leave without keeping a fallback address. The decision feeds your pride without erasing the people who actually housed you.
event.family_civilian_05_business_stewar: The business ledger now contains a page with your name but no job written beside it. The managers offer you the choice to preserve the business, learn elsewhere, or take limited capital to begin differently.
You write 'no position' under your name. The managers have to start from that blank instead of turning the page into automatic succession.
Ask what your share is worth
You ask what the business actually owes you if you take no position. The adults have to separate trust, recommendation, and capital.
Pass the ledger to the employees
You pass the ledger to the employees before signing it. Their reaction is a reminder that your inheritance affects the people who work here too.
Ask for the first shop’s ledger
You ask for the ledger of the shop that already exists before discussing inheritance. The managers have to show what actually works, not just what they plan.
The page waits between employee accounts and supplier accounts. Writing something here does not bind your whole future, but it defines what the business owes you.
The commercial neighborhood now knows you as someone authorized to speak for the family business.
The business turns its name into a recommendation rather than a reserved job.
The managers liquidate a clearly defined share of your stake in the business to fund your own departure.
event.family_civilian_05_adapted_place.t: Before you leave, the household walks you through the adjusted passages, posted service instructions, and redistributed tasks. Nothing forces you to stay, but the house has learned to change around your body instead of deciding for you.
event.family_civilian_05_adapted_place.c: Walk the adapted route once more
You walk the adapted route once more as you have for years. What used to be a problem has become an ordinary rule of the place.
Ask whether the adaptation stays without you
You ask whether the changes will remain after you leave. The household has to decide whether they were only for you or because the old setup was wrong.
Remove your name from the instructions
You remove your name from one posted instruction. If the rule is good, it should survive without being framed as a favor to you.
Ask to post the rule for everyone
You ask for the useful adaptation to become a general posted rule. What began with your body can remain an improvement without belonging to you.
event.family_civilian_05_adapted_place_i: The changes remain even if you leave. The question is whether they become your personal access, a rule for everyone, or simply proof that the household learned to change.
You keep a place already adapted to you and the habit of demanding practical solutions.
The household announces that the adjusted setup and rules will remain available to any worker who needs them.
You leave without claiming the place. What stays with you is the concrete precedent that an organization can change when it harms or excludes.
event.family_civilian_05_neighborhood_na: Your Name in the Neighbors’ Book
After years of favors and arguments, a merchant opens his credit book to a page bearing your name. He makes clear that this trust belongs to you, not automatically to your whole family.
You read the few lines under your name: favors returned, delays owned, disputes settled. The credit rests on specific acts.
Ask who actually honors the credit
You ask which shops actually honor this page. Three names are given; the neighborhood trust stops being a vague promise.
You close the ledger without accepting new debt. The merchant has to explain what remains if you refuse the credit itself.
Record the dispute you refused to judge
You ask the ledger to record the time you refused to lend your name as a verdict. Local trust now includes the boundaries you set.
The book is not official, but several merchants recognize the page. What you accept today will decide how your name travels when you are no longer here every morning.
You gain concrete access to credit because the neighborhood has watched your actions, not because of your social class.
You refuse new debt; what remains is only a local reputation for reliability.
You leave one clearly defined reciprocal favor with the merchants who watched you grow up.
event.family_civilian_05_father_boundary: Your father closes the shop early and sets two bags by the door: one for working tomorrow, the other for leaving when you decide. He refuses to choose yours.
Pack the travel bag with him
You open the travel bag and ask your father what actually belongs in it. For once, he helps you leave instead of teaching you how to stay.
Give him back the work key
You give him back the work key before touching either bag. Your father understands the conversation has to be about your relationship, not your next shift.
Set both bags side by side
You set the two bags side by side until they touch. Your father sees leaving does not automatically erase the possibility of returning.
Recall the empty chair at dinner
You remind your father of the nights work left his chair empty. He understands the travel bag is also about the time you still want to share.
Your father keeps his hands away from both bags. He asks only what the two of you should promise each other before your childhood ends.
Stay his partner, not his employee
Your bond with your father grows stronger because you finally name the difference between helping him and working under his authority.
Your father grips the travel bag before handing it back. His support remains in your relationship even when the shop door closes behind you.
You refuse both bags and the disagreement remains real. You part without false forgiveness, but without pretending the bond is gone.
event.family_civilian_05_two_parent_futu: Your parents place two plans side by side: take on more family work or continue training elsewhere. Neither claims one is more honorable; they simply disagree about the risk.
You swap the two plans in front of your parents to break their camps. Each has to argue for the option they were criticizing a minute ago.
You ask each what they would give up to make the other plan work. The argument leaves principles behind and returns to real costs.
You place a blank sheet between the two plans. Your parents realize they may not have written every option.
Propose a one-month trial away from home
You reuse the idea of a limited trial instead of a permanent choice. Your parents have to judge the plan by what it produces, not by their separate fears.
Your father corrects the cost of the first plan; your mother adds an address to the second. They ask you to choose your future without turning their disagreement into one parent’s victory.
You leave with a concrete address and an imperfect but real family agreement.
You keep recognized access to family work without turning the choice into an imposed career.
You write a third plan that belongs to neither parent's camp. Your parents now have to learn to discuss a future they did not prepare.
event.family_civilian_05_livelihood_fall: The household empties a small cashbox reserved for work expenses and separates what truly belongs to you. There is no ceremony or title: only a few resources and the question of what you still owe the place.
Separate the cash from the tools
You make two piles: what can actually leave with you and what must stay to keep the household running. The share stops being symbolic.
Ask what would still be here if you returned
You ask what the household would guarantee a year from now if you leave with nothing today. The answer has to become more specific than 'we'll see.'
Count it again without claiming anything
You count again so you know what exists, then push your share back. The household has to distinguish declining now from giving it up forever.
Write down what cannot be passed on
You write down the tools, debts, and obligations that must stay with the household. Your share becomes clearer precisely because not everything can leave with you.
The accounts are clear enough to avoid an argument. The household lets you decide whether your share becomes money, future access, or simply a promise to return.
Your share becomes a small real stake, useful enough to matter without buying an entire future.
You take no money, but the household explicitly recognizes your right to return for work.
You claim nothing now and let the household keep its share. You leave the door open to a future conversation instead of forcing a settlement today.
event.family_civilian_05_community_fallb: The Last Round Through the Neighborhood
At thirteen, several neighbors use a delivery round to hand you a letter, a recommendation, or a simple “come see us again.” Nothing is grand; every gesture comes from a relationship actually lived.
You sort the letters by the doors they actually open. The ties become a readable small network instead of a pile of good wishes.
You ask each person what they would actually do for you later. The answers are modest, but specific enough to be kept.
You return the letter promising 'anything you need' without naming anything. The neighbor rewrites it with a real address and a specific kind of help.
Refuse letters with no specific commitment
You keep only the letters that name a concrete form of help. Two neighbors rewrite their promises so they become doors you can actually use.
What the Neighborhood Keeps of You
The round ends at your old door. You can turn those ties into visible reputation, a quiet network, or a specific obligation toward the people who helped you.
The neighborhood speaks about you because it knew you through concrete situations, not because an institution celebrates you.
You keep a quiet network of doors and correspondents without turning it into public reputation.
You turn received help into a specific future obligation, concrete enough to bring the neighborhood back later.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.title: Before Dawn
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.text: A recall order hits the door before dawn. Your father pulls his boots back on under the lamp. There is nobody else to stay with you when he leaves.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn.choic: You clutch his sleeve. Your father stops in the middle of the motion.
You push his boots toward him. He realizes you saw the recall order.
You do not move. Your eyes follow every buckle, button, and movement.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn_i01_t: Your father pauses at the threshold, the folded order in one hand. Outside, the Marine waiting for him avoids looking in.
You tighten your grip. He has to gently pry your fingers loose before leaving.
You hand him what he forgot. He thanks you before stepping outside.
He meets your eyes, then looks down at the order as if he owes an explanation.
event.family_marine_01_before_dawn_i02_a: The door closes. His footsteps fade before the room stops feeling too large.
You refuse to forget that he left despite you.
You put away the rest of his things as if it were already your responsibility.
You remember the door, the lamp, and the sound of his boots.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant.te: A Marine from the neighborhood brings a small blue pennant for the household window. He sets it within reach while speaking with the adult beside you.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant.ch: You grab the blue cloth before the Marine finishes his sentence.
You immediately hand the pennant back to its owner.
Your finger traces the emblem's lines without leaving the cloth.
event.family_marine_01_family_pennant_i0: The Marine crouches to take the pennant back, then pauses when he sees what you are doing.
He laughs and says you already seem to recognize Marine colors.
He nods, surprised by your seriousness.
He names the emblem and shows you where it will be visible from the street.
The pennant is fixed to the window. Passing Marines recognize it at a glance; everyone else looks a little longer.
The symbol quickly becomes something familiar in the household.
You watch the pennant as something that belongs to the adults first.
You memorize the emblem well enough to recognize it elsewhere.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form.te: At the base family check, the clerk stops at a form designed for a Human child. Its chair, ruler, or boxes simply do not match your body.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form.ch: You stay put while he rearranges his equipment around you.
You push away the tool that keeps trying to force you into a measure that does not fit.
You watch the form while the clerk crosses out one box and searches for another.
You deliberately stretch your arm beyond the end of the ruler. The clerk calls someone else over.
event.family_marine_01_no_box_on_form_i0: They Improvise
The clerk gives up on the standard setup. He fetches string, a second stool, and a blank sheet while the line waits behind you.
Show what works
You show him where to place things so they stop getting in your way.
Keep the tool away
You refuse to let him use the old method again, even to save time.
Follow his new notes
You watch the words he invents to replace the crossed-out box.
Ask how far the string goes
The clerk unrolls the entire string. A quartermaster at the far desk turns around.
The Corrected Record
The clerk finally writes something that fits you instead of forcing the old box. The record goes back toward the base archives.
Look at the new entry
For once, the form changes around you.
Turn away from the desk
You leave after forcing the adults to respect a clear boundary.
Remember the correction
You mostly remember the moment the adult had to invent another way to do it.
Watch the quartermaster note your name
The quartermaster writes your name separately before handing the form back.
event.family_marine_04_behind_office_doo: Behind the Office Door
You wait in a base corridor. Behind the door, your father flatly refuses a patrol order. His superior reminds him that a Marine does not choose his missions.
Press your ear to the door
The handle turns while your ear is still against the wood.
You catch a few words, then footsteps approach.
You understand the order concerns civilians your father believes would be endangered.
You hear the order, the refusal, and each man's reason before anyone approaches.
Call your father
You call him before hearing more. The argument stops behind the door.
Back away quietly
Your heel knocks over a bucket in the corridor.
You leave too late: your father spots you at the end of the corridor.
You leave the corridor unseen.
You leave silently and even memorize the route back.
A Few Words Too Many
The word “civilians” carries through the door, then “risk.” Your father answers that an order can be lawful and still be wrong.
Stay to the end
You stay long enough to understand the dispute is about specific people, not your father's pride.
Call him again
Your father finally opens the door. His superior immediately sees you were right outside.
Keep walking
You walk away knowing he said no, but not fully knowing why.
The Door Opens
A few minutes later, your father finds you. He knows you were close enough to understand that he defied a superior.
Ask him why
You ask him directly why he refused.
Pretend you heard nothing
You give him the chance to keep the argument to himself.
Say he was right
You take his side before he has fully explained himself.
Why Did You Say No?
Your father finally chooses what to tell you: the order, the danger he saw, and what a Marine is supposed to do when the two no longer align.
Believe him
You discover that an uniform can contain refusal.
Ask what he risked
You understand his refusal could cost him something real.
Keep your doubt
You mainly remember that the same mission can have two different versions.
event.family_marine_04_dinner_interrupte: Dinner Interrupted
A Marine messenger knocks during dinner. Your father already reaches for his coat; your mother keeps a hand on his bowl and reminds him he promised to stay.
Pull him back to the table
You pull your father toward his chair. Your mother keeps her hand on the bowl.
Push his plate toward him
You push his plate toward his coat as if the choice were already made.
Say “Stay”
Your voice triggers the argument both adults were holding back.
Your father avoids your eyes and keeps hold of his coat.
Your father stops long enough for your mother to speak again.
Your father puts his coat back on the chair. Even the messenger waits for a different answer.
Two Duties
Your father says the patrol is short-handed. Your mother answers that the household is too. The messenger remains at the threshold holding the order.
Stay beside your mother
Your father understands the cost of leaving before he even exits the room.
Hand him his coat
You hand him the coat. Your mother's silence grows heavier.
Ask who is right
The question forces them to explain what each had been demanding from the other.
The Messenger Waits
Nobody can pretend the decision is automatic: the messenger is still waiting, and dinner is getting cold.
Accept that he goes
Your father leaves. Your mother stays beside you until his footsteps fade.
Ask him to stay tonight
Your father returns the order to the messenger and stays, at the cost of an explanation he will owe tomorrow.
Ask him to leave after dinner
The messenger agrees to wait a few minutes. For once, duty and family are not treated as an instant either-or choice.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.title: The Empty Chair
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.text: Your father promised to be there for the neighborhood celebration. The benches fill, the second shift call sounds, and his chair stays empty.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair.choic: You push away the adult's hand when they try to take the chair.
You fold the chair yourself before the celebration ends.
Your voice breaks and several adults stare without knowing what to say.
They tell you a Marine cannot always choose. The chair stays empty.
The neighbor about to move the chair leaves it alone.
The small row around you agrees to keep the seat empty until the end.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair_i01_w: The celebration begins. Music covers the shift bell, but not the empty chair beside you.
You watch every uniform that passes at the end of the street.
You move the chair away so you no longer have to look at it.
Repeat it to anyone who asks
Every time someone asks, you give the same answer: he promised.
event.family_marine_04_empty_chair_i02_t: Your father arrives as the benches are already emptying. He immediately sees the place you kept for him — or the one you put away.
You make him look at the ending celebration before accepting his excuse.
You are still angry, but you refuse to let his lateness erase the rest of the evening.
You head home before he can explain the mission.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_adaptati: In the base mess, the table reserved for families does not fit your body. An adult offers to carry you or move everyone else for you.
You gather what is nearby to make a place that fits you.
You let the adults move what is needed.
You refuse to be carried and stay standing beside the table.
Benches scrape, trays shift, and every eye turns toward the solution you chose.
Nobody had to give up their place, and you did not need to be carried.
The adaptation becomes a shared task instead of a spectacle.
You keep your decision to the end despite the stares.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home.tex: Rain slips under the threshold while your father's service coat is already catching drops. The basin overflows and nobody tells you what to save first.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home.cho: You pull down the coat before it is soaked.
You deal with the overflow first.
You push the water back toward the door with whatever you can find.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_home_i01: When the rain eases, the result of your first choice is obvious in the room.
The coat is dry, but some floorboards are soaked.
You limited the damage by handling the most urgent source first.
Your arms tire before the rain does, but you kept the household afloat.
At pay distribution, a Marine places two nearly identical tokens on the counter: one belongs to your household, the other to an absent family. He asks which one to take.
You invent a difference and choose with far too much confidence.
You hesitate until the Marine takes both tokens back.
You spot a familiar scratch on the right token.
You spot the scratch and a wear mark the Marine had missed.
You immediately choose the wrong token.
You guess wrong and the Marine corrects you before the token leaves the counter.
You guess right without being able to explain why.
You guess right and the Marine laughs at your confidence.
You refuse to choose without proof.
event.family_marine_04_fallback_service_: The Marine finally opens the pay ledger. Small notes beside the numbers explain why the two tokens look alike.
You leave with the right token and a better idea of how the base keeps its accounts.
You accept the written check over your intuition.
You memorize the detail that will let you rely less on someone else next time.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.title: Made to Fit
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.text: A base seamstress opens the seams of a small practice jacket to adapt it to your body. She asks you to show her what gets in the way.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit.choic: Show what gets in the way
You point out where the fabric pulls or blocks.
You test the fastenings one by one instead of making her guess.
You stand as still as you can while she works.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit_i01_f: The first version holds for a few seconds, then a seam pulls, a sleeve catches, or a fastening pops as soon as you move.
You show her the exact movement that makes the jacket fail.
You suggest a different fastening instead of repeating the same setup.
You hold still a few more seconds before admitting it does not work.
event.family_marine_04_made_to_fit_i02_f: The seamstress places the chalk in your hand and asks you to mark what she should change.
The second version works because you helped shape it.
You move until you find the last weak spots, then she fixes them.
You let her apply what she just learned about your body.
Children of Marines chalk out a drill square. When you approach, one blocks the entrance with a stick: “Not with this equipment.”
You take another piece of chalk and start a space beside theirs.
You force your way in and fall in front of everyone.
You step in, but the game stops around you.
You step in and refuse to leave. Eventually the game resumes.
You step in, move two markers, and show everyone another way to continue.
You stay outside the square and memorize their movements.
event.family_marine_04_off_drill_square_: The other children turn toward you. The problem is no longer the equipment: they now have to decide what to do with your presence.
Two children hesitate, then cross the chalk line toward you.
You stay there until someone agrees to resume the game.
From the edge, you copy a drill they just failed.
A Marine stops in front of the two chalk squares. He asks why the group is split before the other children can invent an excuse.
You describe the stick, the equipment, and the refusal. The adult has to answer something concrete.
You point to your own square instead of waiting for the adult to decide for you.
You give him no explanation. The group resumes, but the scene remains entirely between the children.
event.family_marine_04_quartermaster_mea: The Quartermaster's Measure
A quartermaster unrolls his measuring rope to the end, checks your reach, then writes your name in a notebook. At four, he already wants to know how large you will grow.
Stretch out both arms
You deliberately hold the pose and let him record everything.
Ask why
The officer cuts off your question and keeps measuring as if your opinion does not belong in the notebook.
He only says a Giant is “worth tracking.”
He admits some officers track Giant growth for military potential.
You keep asking until he explains what he records, for whom, and why your name matters.
Pull your arm back
You pull your arm back before the final measurement.
The Notebook
When the officer turns the page, you see other large measurements, ages, and notes about expected strength. Your name is not alone.
Look at the other entries
You realize this tracking existed before you and will continue after today.
Close the notebook
You place your hand on the page. The officer has to stop for the first time.
Point at your name
You make it clear you want to know why your name is there.
“Worth Tracking”
The officer finally says it plainly: some superiors want to identify Giants early who might one day serve in Marine forces.
Accept testing, not deciding
You accept being tested, but not having your future decided for you.
Ask who decides for you
You refuse to let the notebook answer for you.
Refuse the tracking
You ask that your name not be used to prepare a career you never chose.
In Front of Your Father
The officer finally asks your father whether he agrees to bring you back. This time, the question is asked in front of you.
Answer before your father
You answer for yourself. The officer writes that down too.
Let your father answer
You watch your father decide what he allows on your behalf.
Refuse yourself
You refuse clearly. Military tracking may continue elsewhere, but not with your consent.
Nobody can watch you today. Your father settles you behind the base storehouse with a box of chalk and tells you not to cross the yellow line.
You turn the box into a small job and stay near the wall.
You take the wrong passage and lose sight of the yellow line immediately.
You go too far before realizing you do not know how to get back.
You learn the rhythm of the corridors and move without being noticed.
You follow the base's movement while always keeping a route back to the storehouse.
The storekeeper gives you string and small tags to carry.
event.family_marine_04_you_come_to_base_: Boots keep crossing the yellow line. Every open door reveals a different piece of the base.
You become useful enough that the adults stop checking where you are every minute.
Keep going to the next corner
You push the exploration to where the corridors become unmistakably military.
People start recognizing you as “the storehouse kid” for the morning.
The Short Siren in the Storehouse
The short siren sounds inside the base storehouse. Marines run toward the yard, and the yellow line your father told you not to cross vanishes under boots and shifted crates.
Look for your father in the yard
You follow the wrong coat and end up in a yard where nobody knows you.
A soldier brings you back to the storehouse before you find your father.
You spot the clearing passages and reach your father without obstructing the alert.
You anticipate the soldiers' movement and reach your father before he can come looking for you.
You stay exactly where you were left, even while everyone runs.
You push small crates and chalk out of the way so the adults can run.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order.title: The Bad Order
event.family_marine_07_bad_order.text: A patrol shuts down a local vendor's stall for a minor violation. Your father enforces the order while the vendor protests that all the goods will spoil by tomorrow.
You stay on the uniformed side while the vendor empties the stall.
Help the vendor save their goods
You start moving what can still be saved before anyone stops you.
Your question lands like an accusation and your father cuts you off in front of everyone.
You are only told that rules are rules.
Your father admits the punishment is broader than the offense.
You force the responsible officer to explain publicly why no middle option exists.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i01_rul: The Signed Order Against the Stall
Your father shows you the signed notice closing the vendor’s stall. The paper is valid; the problem is the food that will spoil today if the order is enforced without flexibility.
Read the signed notice with your father
You verify he did not invent the rule: it really exists.
You separate what can be carried away from what will be lost.
You look for a way to enforce the order without destroying everything on the stall.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i02_per: The vendor places a damaged crate at your feet: even if the order is lifted tomorrow, this part will not come back.
Say that is the price of the rule
You accept that enforcing the rule carries that cost.
You do whatever the order does not explicitly forbid to reduce the damage.
Ask your father if it is fair
You refuse to ask only whether it is legal.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i03_fat: When the stall is empty, your father no longer has the rule in front of him. He now has to answer as your father, not only as a Marine.
You decide the consistency of the rule matters more than what it cost today.
You keep the distinction between obeying correctly and doing something just.
Ask what he would do without the uniform
You force him to separate his personal judgment from the role he just carried out.
event.family_marine_07_fallback_belongin: Finding Your Place
A base activity once again needs adjusting for your body. This time, the adults look directly at you instead of trying to guess what you need.
Say exactly what you need
You give a solution before anyone offers a bad one.
Try their first idea
You agree to test their first idea before judging it.
Adapt on your own
You begin moving the equipment without waiting.
An Imperfect Solution
The first adaptation works halfway. It solves one problem and creates another.
Fix it with them
You explain the new problem before it becomes a new habit.
Make do
You accept an imperfect solution so the activity can continue.
Start over differently
You refuse to let a half-working adaptation become the standard.
Your Way of Doing It
When the activity finally begins, nobody can pretend the solution appeared on its own.
Remember it can be fixed together
You keep the idea that an institution can learn if someone clearly says what does not work.
Remember you can make do
You learn to move forward even when the system only adapts halfway.
Keep your own method
You trust what you build yourself more than solutions designed for you.
event.family_marine_07_fallback_home_dut: Your father leaves three things to do before he returns: close the shutters, fetch water, and keep the meal warm. Only one can be done immediately.
You start by protecting the house.
You start with what will be hardest to replace.
You start with what is directly waiting for your father.
Your father returns earlier than expected and immediately sees the order in which you chose to hold the household together.
You show him you did not forget the other tasks, only chose which one could least afford to wait.
You simply finish the list instead of seeking his approval.
Give one task back to him
You remind him that holding the household together has not become only your job.
event.family_marine_07_fallback_service_: Service as Inheritance
Each year your household must hand a small service record or insignia to the local office. This time, the adult asks you to make the handoff yourself.
Follow the protocol exactly
You repeat the gestures you were shown.
Ask what it is for
You interrupt the ritual before reproducing it.
Add a personal note
You slip something personal into a service formality.
Why We Do It
The clerk explains that the handoff serves both the archives and as a reminder of which families remain tied to service.
Accept the ritual
You understand the gesture exists precisely because it repeats.
Say what it means to you
You refuse to let the office decide alone what the gesture means.
Make the handoff and nothing more
You complete the formality without giving it more weight.
The Gesture That Remains
The clerk files the document. The ritual is over, but you chose whether it belonged mostly to the Marine, your family, or simply the calendar.
Keep it as a Marine tradition
You accept that the institution is part of how your family tells its story.
Keep it as a family tradition
You reclaim the ritual for the household rather than the office.
Treat it as routine
You learn to move through the institution without giving meaning to every gesture.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name.text: An officer praises you in front of other children before the exercise even starts: “With your father's name, we already know what to expect.”
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name.choi: You let the praise land on you as if it already belonged to you.
Say you have done nothing yet
You point out that the name has not passed the exercise for you.
You promise so much that the other children burst out laughing.
Your confidence sounds borrowed rather than convincing.
You turn the praise into a challenge to the group.
Even the officer laughs and asks you to prove that confidence during the exercise.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i01_: Another child says loudly enough to be heard: “They're praising his father. He hasn't done anything.”
You refuse to defend merit you have not earned yet.
You suggest the exercise decide what the name cannot prove.
You openly accept that your family's history already gives you something.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i02_: The drill starts with every eye on you. Every move now seems expected to confirm or deny a story that existed before you.
You miss the simplest move exactly when everyone is watching.
You finish without distinction and without disaster.
You do well enough that the others finally talk about what you did.
You perform clearly well, and your father's name stops being the only thing the officer talks about.
You do only what is required, refusing to turn the drill into a performance.
Help the child who challenged you
You choose to help them with their drill instead of defending your name.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i03_: After the drill, the officer starts talking about your father again. This time, you have something of your own to place beside that name.
You clearly separate what your father did from what you just did.
Say you will carry the name
You accept the name as an expectation, but decide to turn it into a responsibility.
You refuse to let your father's past become a verdict on your future.
event.family_marine_07_giant_demonstrati: The Demonstration
The officers have prepared weights, ropes, and targets to “see where you are.” This time, they ask in front of several adults what you are actually willing to demonstrate.
Do the planned test
You accept the announced program, no more and no less.
Choose the safest exercise
You choose the task least likely to turn your strength into a spectacle.
Ask what the test proves
They answer that the demonstration does not need your opinion to be useful.
The officer vaguely says they need numbers.
He admits they are already comparing your progress to other military profiles.
He explains exactly which performances would trigger closer monitoring.
The Test Begins
The first task looks simple: move a load to a mark without leaving the lane painted on the ground.
Lift cleanly
The load tips and slips from your grip.
You move forward, but the load drifts toward the edge of the lane.
You control the load and still have room to spare.
You finish with enough control that the officers stop talking only about raw strength.
Take more time
You refuse to turn the test into a race and keep the load under control.
Ask for a spotter
You demand a safety measure nobody had planned for the visitors.
The Rope Gives
A restraint rope snaps behind you. A small equipment crate starts sliding toward a young helper standing too close to the area.
Finish your move first
You finish the exercise before turning toward the accident.
Drop the test and protect the helper
You immediately abandon the performance to block the crate's path.
Shout for them to move
You use your voice before your strength to get the helper out of danger.
What Actually Counts
The accident is over. The responsible officer looks first at the timer, then at the helper, then at you.
Defend your choice
You lose your temper and the officer reduces the discussion to your attitude.
He insists the test should have been completed even though nobody was hurt.
You make him admit that a Marine who ignores someone in danger has failed something more important than a timer.
Even the other officers repeat your argument before the supervisor can close the discussion.
Accept their scoring
You let the adults decide the measurable performance was the only important part.
Ask if the helper is okay first
You refuse to discuss the score before checking the person who was endangered.
The Officers Note Your Strength and Judgment
The officers fill out the same kind of notebook they used four years ago. This time, you can see whether they record only the weight you lifted or also the decisions you made during the exercise.
Make them record the protective choice
The note in your file mentions protection before performance.
Make them record the best result
You choose to make the file remember first what your body can do.
Make them record your safety conditions
You make them record that the next demonstration cannot be organized as if nobody else exists around it.
event.family_marine_07_no_return.title: He Doesn't Come Home
event.family_marine_07_no_return.text: Your father's patrol was due back before nightfall. Two hours after the bell, his spare coat still hangs untouched and nobody comes to explain the delay.
You refuse to leave the doorway until you hear his footsteps.
You go looking for someone who has to give you an answer.
You tidy up, heat water, and prepare whatever might help if he returns hurt.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i01_rum: A neighbor says one patrol boat was damaged. He does not know which one or who was aboard.
Your imagination immediately fills in everything the neighbor does not know.
You force the neighbor to admit he is repeating something heard at the port.
You refuse to let the household panic over a story with no names and no proof.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i02_at_: At the base, the guard has no orders to give you information. Behind him, empty stretchers have still been prepared.
The guard sends you home and tells your father you tried to push past him verbally.
The guard repeats the rule without adding a word.
He at least confirms your father is alive and the patrol is returning on foot.
He gives you an estimated return time and confirms your father is escorting an injured Marine.
You sit outside the restricted area and turn waiting into a silent protest.
You leave without a full answer, but with something concrete to do.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i03_ret: Your father finally returns, covered in salt and mud, another Marine's arm over his shoulders. He is not injured, but he immediately sees what his delay did to you.
You do not blame the mission; you blame him for leaving you without knowing.
You put your fear aside until the injured Marine is settled and your father can finally speak.
You refuse reassuring phrases and make him recount the facts in order.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit.te: Despite your earlier refusal, an officer is waiting with three visitors from another service. He presents your size and growth before even asking whether you want to stay.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit.ch: You leave before he finishes the introduction.
Say no in front of them
Your anger lets the officer present your refusal as a tantrum.
He smiles and tries to continue despite your refusal.
The visitors stop and wait for your answer rather than the officer's.
One visitor directly asks why you were brought there without your agreement.
You interrupt the officer and decide what will be shown.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit_i0: The Visitors Wait
The discomfort becomes obvious: the visitors realize they are watching something that was never negotiated with you.
Speak to the visitors, not the officer
You explain directly to them what you are refusing.
Ask them to leave
You change the question: you are no longer the one expected to leave.
Accept one test you choose
You agree to show one thing only because you set the limit.
Saving Face
The officer tries to reframe the scene as a misunderstanding. He wants everyone to leave believing the Marine had planned for your refusal.
Let him save face
You get to leave, but he still gets to explain why.
Correct his version in front of them
You refuse to let your consent be invented after the fact.
Ask where your father is in this decision
You bring the scene back to the family the officer claims to represent.
Your Boundary
The visitors finally leave. What remains matters more for the future: the officer now knows exactly what boundary you set and whether he respected it.
State what cannot happen again
You turn your refusal into an explicit rule for any future summons.
Decide not to cooperate again
You now refuse any tracking that begins without your agreement.
Only agree when you present yourself
You keep the door open only if nobody speaks about you before you do.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.title: Not on the List
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.text: At an activity reserved for Marine families, the organizer looks for your name and stops: the column for your equipment or body type is blank.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.choic: The organizer bristles and says he cannot rewrite the list for one person.
He promises to think about it next time, which solves nothing today.
He agrees to make a temporary place for you today.
He changes the list in front of you and asks what equipment is actually needed.
You suggest a version your body can actually take part in.
You refuse to stand around waiting for a box to appear for you.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i01_p: The other families wait while the organizer decides: include you, improvise something, or continue without you.
You refuse to let the decision be made away from you.
You take the equipment and show exactly what needs to change.
You leave before the adults turn your absence into a minor logistical detail.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i02_o: The other children realize the decision made about you may change the activity for them too.
Invite them to try your version
A few try your adaptation and discover it works for them too.
Ask only for your own place
You refuse to prove the solution benefits everyone just to deserve a place.
The activity resumes, but your absence becomes visible instead of disappearing into an empty box.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i03_r: At the end, the organizer keeps the sheet. He has to decide what he will write for next time.
Make sure he changes the list
Your name and a concrete solution remain on the sheet after you leave.
You leave mainly knowing you can make your own place without waiting for perfect permission.
You do not forget how easily the organization continued without you.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant.text: An old sergeant recognizes your name during a base formality. He says he served with your father and asks whether anyone ever told you “the broken bridge story.”
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant.choi: The sergeant smiles as if he knows exactly which version you expect.
You ask him to leave out plaques, ranks, and polished words.
Say you do not want to hear it
