event.family_pirate_10_fallback_legacy_i: The Value Is Not in the Wood
The chest stays in the household. The buyer admits he recognizes two old wanted pirates. The chest is valuable mostly as a lead to people, debts, and perhaps still-active caches.
You keep the names and lose the money you needed now.
The Value Is Not in the Wood
You understand what he is really buying. The buyer admits he recognizes two old wanted pirates. The chest is valuable mostly as a lead to people, debts, and perhaps still-active caches.
Ask why he wants the names
The offer becomes an information trade, not a furniture sale.
The Value Is Not in the Wood
The chest leaves. The buyer admits he recognizes two old wanted pirates. The chest is valuable mostly as a lead to people, debts, and perhaps still-active caches.
The money solves an immediate problem while family names change hands.
event.family_pirate_13_flag_means_mine.t: An old family crewmate unfolds a piece of the old black flag, burned along one edge. He puts it in front of you without an oath: “You decide what it means now.”
event.family_pirate_13_flag_means_mine.c: Take it and choose the sea
You take the burned scrap and tie it to your pack; the old crewmate asks for no further oath.
Keep the cloth, not the career
You put the cloth with your personal belongings rather than with the gear for departure.
You fold the flag carefully and return it to its box without giving an answer about your future career.
event.family_pirate_13_flag_means_mine_i: You claim the cloth as inheritance and say your Active life will begin as a pirate, on your own terms. The crewmate tells one victory and one wrong committed beneath the same flag. He does not ask you to love one in order to keep the memory of the other.
Take it and choose the sea
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a pirate carrying this scrap without inheriting the old flag's wrongs.

You keep the cloth as proof of where you come from without making it your profession at fifteen. The crewmate tells one victory and one wrong committed beneath the same flag. He does not ask you to love one in order to keep the memory of the other.
Keep the cloth, not the career
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian; the scrap will remain family inheritance, not recruitment.

You put the flag away without answering forever. The crewmate tells one victory and one wrong committed beneath the same flag. He does not ask you to love one in order to keep the memory of the other.
You do not take the patch. The flag remains an open question the crew remembers leaving to you.
event.family_pirate_13_safe_harbor_key.t: The Key to a Changed Door
The former keeper of a safe house gives you a bent key. The house has a new owner, but the key still bears the notches once used to recognize allies.
event.family_pirate_13_safe_harbor_key.c: You put the key around your neck and ask the keeper which name still answers to the old notches.
You close your hand around the key without asking for the address of any current refuge.
You put the key away and refuse to let the keeper notify anyone that you came.
event.family_pirate_13_safe_harbor_key_i: You take the key as the first tool of a pirate life, not as a promise that every door belongs to you. The keeper reminds you how many people lied, paid, or took risks to keep that door safe. An escape network protects people; it also burdens those who maintain it.
You return the key after memorizing the signals. The safe-harbor network now agrees to recognize you.

You keep the key as memory of a lost refuge and choose to begin Active as a civilian. The keeper reminds you how many people lied, paid, or took risks to keep that door safe. An escape network protects people; it also burdens those who maintain it.
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian; the key will remain a memory of a lost refuge.

You keep the key without taking over the network. The keeper reminds you how many people lied, paid, or took risks to keep that door safe. An escape network protects people; it also burdens those who maintain it.
You do not take the key. You keep the sign and address; the refuge's banded gull follows when you leave.
event.family_pirate_13_ledger_of_names.t: While clearing the household's last belongings, you find a ledger where loot, debts, and former owners share the same pages. Several names have been crossed out without explanation.
event.family_pirate_13_ledger_of_names.c: You slide the ledger into your travel pack and mark the first page that will need checking.
Keep it to understand the debts
You separate the debt pages from the loot accounts and start a list of names to find.
You tie the ledger shut and put your own knot across the cover before storing it.
event.family_pirate_13_ledger_of_names_i: You take the ledger and choose a pirate career that will have to answer to those names rather than erase them. A final page separates what was returned, repaid, abandoned, or never made right. The family did sometimes know its prizes continued to have owners.
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a pirate with these names to investigate rather than erase.

You keep the accounts as a historical debt but refuse to turn them into recruitment. A final page separates what was returned, repaid, abandoned, or never made right. The family did sometimes know its prizes continued to have owners.
Keep it to understand the debts
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian and pursue the ledger's debts without joining a crew.
You seal the ledger for later. A final page separates what was returned, repaid, abandoned, or never made right. The family did sometimes know its prizes continued to have owners.
You leave the ledger sealed with a keeper. You know where to recover it without carrying it.
event.family_pirate_13_mothers_salt_char: Your Mother’s Salt-Stained Chart
A long-delayed package contains your mother's chart, stained with salt, crossed-out ports, and three routes marked in her own hand. Nothing says when she will return.
Follow her route as a pirate
You spread the chart across your table and circle the first route you want to follow for yourself.
Keep the chart without following it
You store the chart with her letters instead of placing it among navigation charts.
Choose later
You fold the chart over the crossed-out ports and leave all three routes unmarked.
Your Mother’s Chart Is Not an Order
You take your mother’s salt-stained chart to begin Active as a pirate at fifteen, not to copy her voyage. In the margin, she warns that a safe route today can become a trap tomorrow.
Follow her route as a pirate
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a pirate by following your own route across your mother's chart.
A Route Is Not an Order

You keep her annotations as family memory and decide to begin Active as a civilian at fifteen. In the margin, she wrote that a safe route today may be a trap tomorrow. Even her best maritime inheritance has to be judged again by the person receiving it.
Keep the chart without following it
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian; the chart will remain a link to your mother, not an order to depart.
A Route Is Not an Order

You refuse to let an absence decide for you. In the margin, she wrote that a safe route today may be a trap tomorrow. Even her best maritime inheritance has to be judged again by the person receiving it.
Choose later
You leave the chart safe, but remember where it will wait if you ever choose to follow it.
event.family_pirate_13_crew_has_limits.t: After years of disputes between home and crew, an old pirate carves three rules into a plank: no weapons in the bedroom, no plan without household consent, no child used as cover.
event.family_pirate_13_crew_has_limits.c: You take the plank and add your own mark beneath the three rules before packing it with your things.
You hang the plank in the common room exactly where the crew will see it when they enter.
You leave the plank against the wall and refuse to carve any promise about your future profession into it.
event.family_pirate_13_crew_has_limits_i: You take the plank as a principle for a chosen pirate career, not as an excuse for everything else. Nobody claims these rules make pirates good. They only state which limits this family learned because living without them already cost something.
You carry the code, not a patch. Pirates around the circle begin to recognize those limits as yours.

You keep the rules for the household and choose to begin Active as a civilian. Nobody claims these rules make pirates good. They only state which limits this family learned because living without them already cost something.
You refuse to let pirate code rule the household. 7,500 Berrys are set aside for your future civilian departure.
You refuse to commit your future today. Nobody claims these rules make pirates good. They only state which limits this family learned because living without them already cost something.
You do not adopt the code yet. The crew still remembers that you demanded limits before answering.
The Share That Was Never Yours
The family ledger lets you find someone whose property helped fund your household. She agrees to meet and places on the table the same receipt you saw as a child.
Repay the share, then go pirate
You push the agreed amount toward the former owner and keep the original receipt for yourself.
Repay the share and stay civilian
You repay the share and ask for the receipt to be crossed out in front of both of you.
You put no money on the table; the receipt stays between you, uncrossed.
event.family_pirate_13_return_the_share_: You settle what you can and still choose piracy, carrying a specific debt instead of a clean story. Returning the money or item does not restore the lost years. The person accepts it anyway, then asks what you intend to do with what your family taught you.
Repay the share, then go pirate
The debt is settled and the receipt crossed out. In this pirate network, people now know you repay what your family owes.

You return the share and choose to begin Active as a civilian without erasing your affection for your family. Returning the money or item does not restore the lost years. The person accepts it anyway, then asks what you intend to do with what your family taught you.
Repay the share and stay civilian
You settle the debt without joining the crew. The crossed-out receipt matters more than the ledger you refuse to carry.

You refuse to turn an incomplete repayment into a ceremony. Returning the money or item does not restore the lost years. The person accepts it anyway, then asks what you intend to do with what your family taught you.
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian with a family debt still unresolved.
event.family_pirate_13_no_innocents_code: The Black Flag’s Red Line
A family veteran gives you a piece of flag with words stitched inside: “Not the innocent.” He admits the crew did not always obey its own rule.
Choose piracy under that rule
You take the flag scrap and trace the stitched words 'Not innocents' with a finger before folding it.
Keep the rule without becoming pirate
You copy the sentence onto a fresh sheet and hand the flag back to the veteran.
Reject the symbol, not the family
You push the flag away but keep the sheet where the rule was copied.
A Rule Matters When It Is Hard

You choose a pirate career and take the flag as a rule to uphold when it truly costs something. The veteran names the moment the crew broke the rule to profit faster. The code erases neither victim nor choice; it only gives you a line to defend tomorrow.
Choose piracy under that rule
You take that principle to sea without turning a patch into morality. Pirates now know the line you claim.
A Rule Matters When It Is Hard

You keep the rule as moral inheritance without accepting the pirate career today. The veteran names the moment the crew broke the rule to profit faster. The code erases neither victim nor choice; it only gives you a line to defend tomorrow.
Keep the rule without becoming pirate
You keep the principle without keeping the flag. Those who heard your decision know where you draw the line.
A Rule Matters When It Is Hard

You reject the symbol without rejecting the people you love. The veteran names the moment the crew broke the rule to profit faster. The code erases neither victim nor choice; it only gives you a line to defend tomorrow.
Reject the symbol, not the family
You refuse to let the flag turn a minimum rule into virtue. That distance becomes known.
event.family_pirate_13_own_depth.title: Your Own Depth
event.family_pirate_13_own_depth.text: The crew offers you an old diver's bell, used to signal that an underwater job is willingly accepted. “Nobody ties it to you. You ring it, or you don't.”
You ring the old bell once; the crew waits for you to state what that signal will mean.
Keep the bell and stay civilian
You take the bell without ringing it and store it with your personal belongings.
You leave the bell silent on the table; nobody ties the prepared rope beside it to you.
event.family_pirate_13_own_depth_i01_pir: You ring once and choose to begin Active as a pirate at fifteen under conditions that belong to you. The bell is heavy in your hand and useless without your action. After years of adults confusing ability with availability, that difference is finally made physical.
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a pirate while keeping the right to decide when the bell rings.
event.family_pirate_13_own_depth_i01_kee: You keep the bell as proof that your ability belongs to you. The bell is heavy in your hand and useless without your action. After years of adults confusing ability with availability, that difference is finally made physical.
Keep the bell and stay civilian
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian; the bell will remain proof that your ability belongs to you.
event.family_pirate_13_own_depth_i01_ref: You do not ring it. The bell is heavy in your hand and useless without your action. After years of adults confusing ability with availability, that difference is finally made physical.
You leave the bell and refuse to make your body a crew tool. Those offering the job remember your boundary.
A family contact gives you a small card bearing three names, each tied to a refuge that once helped your people. Two names are crossed out; the third is still good today.
Take the network and go pirate
You copy the third name onto a fresh card and ask how to contact them without exposing the two lost refuges.
You keep the entire card, crossed-out names included, without sending a message to the last contact.
You fold and seal the card; the family contact leaves without warning the third name.
event.family_pirate_13_fallback_pursuit_: You accept the network as a tool of a chosen pirate career, with its concrete obligations. The contact insists: no name is an infinite resource. Every refuge belongs to someone who may agree, refuse, betray, or ask for something in return.
Take the network and go pirate
You memorize the signals instead of carrying the key. The safe-harbor network now recognizes you as one of its own.

You keep the last refuge's key without entering the career. The contact insists: no name is an infinite resource. Every refuge belongs to someone who may agree, refuse, betray, or ask for something in return.
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian and keep the last contact as unused inheritance.
You keep the name without using it. The contact insists: no name is an infinite resource. Every refuge belongs to someone who may agree, refuse, betray, or ask for something in return.
You do not take the key. You keep only the sign and address, enough to find the harbor later.
event.family_pirate_13_fallback_househol: The Piece That Stays Home
As your fifteenth year approaches, a piece of the family flag is cut in two. One half stays in the home; the other is placed in front of you without demand.
Take your half to sea
You take the half set before you and slip it into your departure pack; the other remains pinned at home.
Leave both at home
You place the two halves together on the table and leave them both in the house.
Keep your half without choosing piracy
You fold your half small enough for a pocket without attaching it to any flag.
Family and Crew Are Not the Same Word

You take your half and choose to begin Active as a pirate at fifteen. The adult cutting the cloth says a household can love a pirate without becoming their crew, and a child can love the household without taking up the same profession.
Take your half to sea
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a pirate with one half of the flag while the other stays at home.
Family and Crew Are Not the Same Word
Both pieces stay home. The adult cutting the cloth says a household can love a pirate without becoming their crew, and a child can love the household without taking up the same profession.
Leave both at home
You leave the patch at home. A 7,500-Berry purse becomes the practical help you will leave with at fifteen.
Family and Crew Are Not the Same Word

You keep the cloth in your pocket without accepting the career. The adult cutting the cloth says a household can love a pirate without becoming their crew, and a child can love the household without taking up the same profession.
Keep your half without choosing piracy
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian with the cloth in your pocket, without turning it into a flag.
event.family_pirate_13_fallback_legacy.t: What the Ledger Does Not Forgive
The final family ledger fits in one hand. It contains gains, losses, allies' names, and property never returned; no page reduces the family to heroes or monsters.
event.family_pirate_13_fallback_legacy.c: You put the ledger in your bag and mark the pages you refuse to forget.
You store the ledger with your personal papers rather than in a crew chest.
You close the ledger and tie its strap without choosing which page will guide your adult life.
event.family_pirate_13_fallback_legacy_i: You take the ledger and choose a pirate career that will have to live with everything inside it. The last page is blank. It does not erase the earlier ones; it only shows your professional choice can begin after this history instead of being written by it.
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a pirate with the whole ledger, including its shameful pages.

You keep the ledger and choose to begin Active as a civilian without pretending to come from another family. The last page is blank. It does not erase the earlier ones; it only shows your professional choice can begin after this history instead of being written by it.
At fifteen, you intend to begin as a civilian without filing the ledger outside your own history.
You close the ledger without a promise. The last page is blank. It does not erase the earlier ones; it only shows your professional choice can begin after this history instead of being written by it.
You leave the ledger closed with your family. The inheritance remains accessible, but no page decides for you yet.
event.family_revolutionary_01_wealthy_do: In the family dining room, a guest slips an envelope under a plate while an organizer quietly thanks the household. A house servant moves in to clear the table before the money is hidden.
You grab the envelope; the organizer immediately reaches to take it back.
You push the plate over the envelope; the servant stops with her hand still out.
You offer the envelope to the servant; the donor abruptly rises from his chair.
The donor wants the envelope back without explaining it. The servant hesitates in front of you while the household adults must choose between their respectable façade and clandestine support.
Hold it out to an adult
You hold the envelope out to a household adult; they take it back and keep the servant out of the secret.
You let the envelope fall on the table. An adult now has to move it in full view.
You hold it to your chest; the adults have to wait instead of making someone else carry the act.
event.family_revolutionary_01_mothers_bu: By the door, your mother sews three different-colored buttons onto a courier's coat. When someone knocks twice outside, she hides the needle but leaves the coat on your lap.
You clutch the coat to yourself; your mother steps between the door and your lap.
You tug a colored button; the thread snaps just as the handle moves.
You point at the door; your mother immediately puts out the lamp beside the coat.
Your mother recognizes the signal but cannot know whether the person outside is the right contact. The coded coat is still with you and the courier waits in the next room.
Hold the coat to your mother
You hold the coat toward your mother; she takes it back before cracking the door open.
Push the coat under the bench
You push the coat beneath the bench; your mother leaves the hiding place as the handle moves.
Hold the coat on your lap
You keep the coat on your lap; your mother does not open while the buttons remain visible.
event.family_revolutionary_01_two_parent: At the kitchen table, your father holds a rolled map while your mother wants it burned before dawn. They stop arguing when you catch the paper's edge between their two cups.
The map slides toward your father; your mother moves her cup before it spills.
The roll touches your mother's hand; your father loosens his grip without looking away.
You crumple the map between them; both parents release it to stop your hands.
The map marks a house where someone must sleep tonight. Your father wants to keep the route in case it is needed; your mother refuses to let an address endanger a family if the house is searched.
Hold the paper to your father
You hold the paper toward your father; he copies a few landmarks while your mother keeps the stove open.
Push the paper toward the stove
You push the map toward the heat; your mother burns it and your father puts his pencil away.
Pull the paper with both hands
You pull at the middle; your parents finish separating the route from the address.
event.family_revolutionary_01_orphan_spa: In the room where the cell lets you sleep, a woman slips a key under your pillow before leaving to open the back door. Another adult objects to using your bed as a hiding place.
You close your hand around the key; both adults stop arguing to look at you.
The key clatters on the floor; someone immediately bends to pick it up.
You pull the pillow close; the protesting adult blocks the woman from taking it back.
Your Bed Is Not a Lockbox
The key opens a small refuge's back exit. The adults need to leave soon, but one insists that sheltering you here does not give them the right to use your things as clandestine storage.
Hold the key out to the adult
You hold out the key; the adult takes it back and stops using your pillow as a hiding place.
Put the key in the box
You put the key in the empty box; the adults leave it there, away from your bed.
Keep the key in your hand
You refuse to let go of the key; the adults wait until departure before taking it back.
event.family_revolutionary_01_poor_relie: In a relief line outside a warehouse, a volunteer fills your family's bowl and chalks a small mark underneath. A neighbor asks why only some bowls are being marked.
You rub the bowl's underside; the volunteer immediately crouches to see what you are erasing.
You turn the bowl toward the neighbor; several people in line see the mark at once.
You hold the bowl close; the volunteer stops trying to take it back to finish her ledger.
The volunteer says the mark helps find families for the next distribution. A man behind her adds that the same families could also 'return the favor' later.
You hold the bowl close; the volunteer leaves the food and crosses out the future-services column.
You rub until the chalk mark disappears; nobody takes back the ration already served.
You point at the register instead of your bowl; the volunteer keeps only the distribution address.
event.family_revolutionary_01_shutter_ma: At dawn, an adult draws a short chalk line on the house shutter and hides the chalk in a sleeve. When you touch the mark, the adult immediately checks both ends of the street.
Your finger smears the line; the adult catches the shutter before you wipe it all away.
You add a second line; the adult's eyes widen and a cloth comes out immediately.
You tap the glass; someone waiting at the corner turns toward the house.
The line means a message may be dropped today. Your imitation has made the code ambiguous, and the person at the corner no longer knows whether to approach.
You rub until the signal disappears; the adult does not redraw it.
You tap the first line; the adult wipes away your copy and keeps only the intended code.
You push the shutter closed; the signal disappears and the person at the corner leaves.
event.family_revolutionary_04_donor_ledg: In the family office, an organizer puts a ledger before the person managing household resources: one column for donations, another for 'available' homes and vehicles. An employee's name is already in the second.
You circle the name; the employee recognizes her copied handwriting and asks who entered it.
You shut the ledger; the organizer keeps a hand on it instead of reopening it.
You put a coin on the donations column; the adult keeping the accounts shifts the ledger to separate money from people.

The employee says she may drive sometimes, but never agreed to be listed as a permanent resource. The organizer replies that the household already funds the cell and it must be able to count on 'everything that comes with it.'
Two pages replace the columns: money can be pledged without automatically committing employees' labor.
The employee's name is crossed out; each ride must be requested directly from the person involved.
The ledger stays intact; the employee now knows her job and the household's political support are being mixed.
event.family_revolutionary_04_mothers_sp: The Bed Taken for the Night
Your mother opens your small room to an injured courier and starts moving your blankets without warning. The courier says he can sleep on the floor; she answers that the cell has nowhere else safe.
You clutch the blanket; your mother stops pulling and the courier steps back toward the door.
You point to the floor; the courier sits there before your mother can decide for you.
You bring a pillow; your mother understands that helping did not mean offering the entire bed.
The courier must stay hidden until morning. Your mother finally asks what you are willing to share; outside, a patrol passes down the street and narrows the options.
Keep the bed, lend the floor
The courier takes the floor and a spare blanket; your room helps without becoming cell property.
You agree he can sleep in the room tonight; your mother promises to ask before the next emergency.
Move the courier to the kitchen
The table is pushed to the wall and the kitchen becomes the refuge, leaving your child's space intact.
event.family_revolutionary_04_parents_sa: The Door That Must Stay Family
Your father wants the back door left unlocked for a late contact. Your mother refuses: a neighbor has already noticed nighttime visitors. They find you holding the key while arguing in the hall.
Your father takes the key, but your mother blocks the door before he can open it.
Your mother closes her hand around the key; your father goes to check the back window.
Hide the key in your pocket
You hide the key; both parents have to stop deciding as though it were just a detail.
A Home Is Not a Passage
The contact may be in danger if the door stays shut, but opening the home exposes the whole family. Your parents look for a solution that treats neither side as disposable.
Your father places a discreet marker farther away; the family door stays locked until confirmation.
Your mother agrees to one opening at a fixed time, then the key returns inside immediately.
Close the house to the network
The contact will need another refuge; your walls stop being treated as an automatic passage.
event.family_revolutionary_04_orphan_gua: At the back of a clinic, a revolutionary fills out your medical form and writes his own name under 'guardian.' The medic asks whether he actually lives with you; he hesitates before answering.
You tap the box; the medic takes the form back before he can invent an address.
You draw across the name; the revolutionary sets down his pencil and lets you finish.
You point to yourself; the medic writes a separate note instead of inventing a family on the form.
A Box Does Not Make a Parent
The medic can record an emergency contact without pretending he is your parent. The revolutionary admits that a network sheltering you is not automatically a family.
The form names one precise responsibility without artificially giving you a parent.
The guardian box stays blank and the medic keeps only the information needed for care.
The name is paired with a written limit: responsible only for this medical visit.
event.family_revolutionary_04_ration_deb: At the distribution, a coordinator records how many sacks your family received, then adds a 'future help' column. A poor neighbor objects: nobody mentioned service in exchange before the baskets were filled.
You rub at the charcoal column; the coordinator grabs the ledger before the names disappear too.
Put the sack on the ledger
You put the sack on the open book; the neighbor laughs and the coordinator has to move it to continue.
You share a handful; the neighbor keeps it without looking at the debt column.
The coordinator says he is only noting 'reliable' people. The neighbor demands a choice: distribute aid, or recruit openly, but do not mix the two afterward.
The column disappears; families keep the sacks already given with no added obligation.
A second sheet appears at the other end of the table; nobody is listed unless they come forward themselves.
The ledger keeps both columns; your family now knows this aid may later be invoked as a debt.
event.family_revolutionary_04_aid_withou: In a shelter, a volunteer puts a contact form beneath every soup bowl. A displaced family refuses to give an address; the cook keeps filling their bowl anyway.
You slide the sheet off the table; the bowl stays exactly where the cook placed it.
You stack the blank forms; the volunteer can no longer slip them quietly under the bowls.
You point to the bowl; the cook says aloud that the soup has no conditions.
The shelter decides to physically separate relief from recruitment. The question becomes simple: what information is actually needed to feed and house people today?
Relief forms now ask only what is needed for food, housing, and care.
Recruitment moves to the back of the room, visible but separate from bowls and beds.
Families can leave the address blank without losing their place in line.
event.family_revolutionary_04_giant_floo: The Floorboards That Speak Too Loudly
Agents hide pamphlets beneath thin floorboards. When you step forward, your Giant weight makes the boards groan and lifts a corner of the rug; someone in the street stops by the window.
You step back; the floor stops creaking, but the rug stays lifted over the cache.
You sit on a solid patch; outside, the figure keeps watching the window.
You pull the rug down by hand; the pamphlets vanish just before someone knocks on the shutter.
Adapt the Hiding Place, Not Your Body
The adults realize the hiding place requires you to move as though your body were the problem. They need to relocate the pamphlets before the next visit.
Move the cache into the wall
The pamphlets move into a wall niche; your footsteps no longer act as an accidental alarm.
The adults reinforce the area instead of ordering you to avoid it.
The room stops serving as clandestine storage; nobody asks you to become smaller to protect the secret.
event.family_revolutionary_04_household_: An adult fills the hall cupboard with coats and papers belonging to people staying overnight. Your childhood things are pushed into a basket on the floor without anyone asking you.
You pull the basket close; several coats fall and an adult has to catch them.
You open the doors wide; the visitors immediately see what displaced your things.
You put a coat on a chair; its owner comes to take it instead of leaving the decision to the adult.
The improvised refuge needs storage, but not permanent rights over every piece of family furniture. The adults must redistribute their things before night.
One shelf remains for the family; the rest serves visitors until morning.
Everyone stores their own things in a named box instead of displacing yours without a trace.
The cupboard can help tonight, but clandestine storage does not automatically become permanent.
event.family_revolutionary_04_network_fa: A stranger has waited on the bench beneath the window for too long. The refuge adult says he knows 'someone in the network,' but nobody in the room recognizes his face.
You pull the curtain; the stranger looks up at the window that just vanished.
You tap the known signal; the stranger does not answer and shifts on the bench.
Pull the adult to the window
You pull the adult to the curtain; he finally looks for himself before opening anything.
A Network Is Not a Password
The refuge refuses to open on a mere verbal recommendation. They must decide how to verify a contact without turning your presence—or another child's—into a trust test.
The stranger leaves when he cannot give the second half of the signal.
An adult leaves by the back to verify his identity away from the refuge door.
The door stays shut; the network will have to fix its own verification failure.
event.family_revolutionary_07_respectabl: During a respectable reception, an organizer sends three couriers through the servants' entrance disguised as deliveries. An employee discovers her name on the false receipts without ever being asked.
Take the receipt from the courier
You take the receipt; the courier stops at the service door and the employee finally sees her name.
You call the employee over; the organizer can no longer use her signature as silent cover.
You point toward the front entrance; a parent realizes the family's respectability will have to carry its own risk.
The operation can still continue, but the employee refuses to be officially responsible for access she never accepted. The network must decide who signs and who controls the cover.
The false receipts now bear the name of the household that chose the risk, not an employee drafted by default.
The employee agrees to one passage and sets the time herself; employment is not permanent consent.
The couriers leave by another route; the reception stays respectable without turning staff into human cover.
event.family_revolutionary_07_code_in_sc: Your mother slips a coded strip into the lining of your schoolbag before school. When you ask why, she says a child draws less attention than an adult courier.
You pull the paper out in front of her; your mother has to answer before she can close the lining.
You put the bag down and refuse to take it; your mother is left holding the message she wanted moved.
You ask for the recipient's name; your mother realizes she was about to send you without telling you to whom.
Less Visible Does Not Mean Available
Your mother admits the network is using your age to lower suspicion. She must decide whether urgency truly justifies turning you into discreet transport.
Remove the message from the bag
The paper goes back with an adult; your school route stops being an operational route chosen without you.
You accept this specific trip after getting the destination and fallback plan; it is not blanket permission.
Your mother hides the paper in a fixed dead drop an adult will retrieve later. It is her final relay from the household before leaving, without using your schoolbag.
event.family_revolutionary_07_split_inst: The False Name Asked at Dinner

At dinner, your father asks you to introduce a visitor under a false name. Your mother interrupts him: protecting the cell, she says, should not force you to lie in your own kitchen. The visitor waits.
You use the false name; your father nods while your mother stays silent in front of the visitor.
You introduce the visitor without naming him; both parents realize you made your own rule.
You ask the visitor what he wants to be called; the decision stops belonging only to your parents.
The visitor explains the false name protects him, but he does not want children forced to lie for him. Your parents must distinguish safety from family obedience.
You agree false names may be used in the house without requiring you to invent extra stories.
Your father takes responsibility for explanations; you are no longer tasked with making the lie convincing.
Your mother tells the visitor that adults will carry the risks of the cover themselves.
event.family_revolutionary_07_guardian_p: An organizer prepares an evacuation and wants to list the same revolutionary as guardian for every parentless child in the refuge. You recognize the name from the clinic and ask whether he will actually travel with you.
You scan the names; several children are assigned to the same adult who is not even in the room.
You cross out the column; the organizer stops writing and asks how escorts should be identified instead.
Your question forces the organizer to bring out the actual escort list rather than the administrative list of fake guardians.
A Refuge Must Know Who Is Responsible
The evacuation needs clear responsibilities, not a fictional family printed on every form. Adults must list escorts, contacts, and handoff points separately.
The forms state who travels with each child without pretending that person becomes their parent.
Each leg has a distinct responsible adult; nobody is made universal guardian for convenience.
Keep a copy of your route
You receive a simple copy of the names and handoff points so you know who is supposed to be responsible for you.
event.family_revolutionary_07_relief_nam: After a distribution, an organizer asks for the list of aided families for a leaflet praising revolutionary action. A woman from your neighborhood refuses to be used as an example while she still hides her rent debt from the landlord.
You place a blank sheet over the column; the organizer can see only the quantities distributed.
You tear the copy carrying the names; the woman collects the pieces where hers appeared.
You show only the sack totals; the organizer realizes the aid can be reported without exposing recipients.
Aid Does Not Grant Story Rights
The leaflet can mention the distribution without identifying recipients. The movement must decide whether to lose a more emotional story to protect the people involved.
The leaflet gives place, quantity, and remaining needs; no family becomes political proof without consent.
Only people who volunteer appear; receiving a sack does not authorize anyone to speak for them.
The distribution remains useful even without a public story to showcase it.
event.family_revolutionary_07_aid_regist: The shelter separated relief from recruitment, but an organizer now proposes copying the same addresses into both ledgers 'to save time.' The cook refuses to hand over the recipients' book.
You keep the relief ledger against you; the organizer cannot copy any address without taking it from you.
You swap the covers to show how similar the books look; the cook demands a distinct code.
You put a blank ledger before the organizer; if he wants to recruit, he must build his own list.
Separate the Data Like the Tables
The shelter must make its separation real in the records. Otherwise relief remains a back door into a political file recipients never chose.
The two ledgers share no address without explicit consent from the person concerned.
An address enters the political ledger only if the person explicitly requests the transfer.
Notes already linking relief and recruitment are burned in front of both teams.
event.family_revolutionary_07_search_at_: A Marine patrol knocks while a clandestine visitor removes muddy shoes in the hall. The soles leave a trail toward the room where papers were just hidden.
You wipe the first print; behind the door, the patrol knocks a second time.
You shove the shoes under a cabinet; the visitor retreats in socks toward the back room.
You open an empty room near the hall; an adult moves the conversation there before answering the door.
The patrol says it is looking for a clandestine printer. The household can mislead it, limit the search, or sacrifice material so residents do not become the price of the cache.
The adult opens the hall but refuses bedroom access without clear authority, taking the confrontation personally.
The most dangerous papers disappear into the stove before the patrol gets farther.
The visitor leaves through a prepared back exit; residents do not become human shields for his escape.
event.family_revolutionary_07_false_name: The List That Accuses Too Quickly
An organizer compares the shelter list with a police report and circles three names as 'possible informants.' One belongs to a woman who simply refused to join the cell after receiving aid.
You point to the name and ask why; the organizer finds only a note saying 'refuses to commit.'
You erase the circle; the woman stops being marked by a simple pencil stroke.
You pull the papers apart; the organizer has to explain what truly connects each name to the police report.
The cell must decide whether to keep suspicions with no evidence. A false accusation can protect a network for hours and ruin a person for years.
Names without concrete evidence are removed from the alert list.
The report is isolated until reviewed by someone outside the original accusation.
The names remain circled; the network chooses caution at the cost of suspicion that may become its own evidence.
event.family_revolutionary_07_household_: The Drawer That Will Not Close
The family drawer will no longer close: false papers, keys, and messages have displaced household letters and small belongings. An adult suggests emptying the rest to make room.
You put the clandestine papers on the table; their volume can no longer be treated as a domestic detail.
You rescue the family letters before an adult pushes them into an unlabeled basket.
You put a box in the middle of the drawer; the adults understand the idea immediately.
A Home Keeps Its Own Things Too
The cell needs hiding places, but the household needs places that do not slowly become clandestine offices. Adults must set a material boundary.
Limit the cell to one drawer
One area is reserved for clandestine papers; the rest clearly returns to the household.
The documents leave the house for a safe box outside the home.
Return the drawer to the family
The cell must find another place; this piece of furniture stops becoming organizational property by accumulation.
event.family_revolutionary_07_network_fa: A courier arrives at the refuge with the correct coded phrase but no recipient name. Two adults want to open it 'so the information is not lost,' though nobody knows who it was meant for.
You keep the note sealed; the courier stops offering it to adults volunteering to open it.
You ask for the last handoff; the courier can at least name the house where he received it.
You hand the note back; the courier realizes a correct code phrase does not create a recipient.
The network must choose between speed and chain of responsibility. Opening the note may help, but it destroys the rule that tells anyone who was supposed to read it.
An adult goes to verify the handoff chain; the note stays sealed until then.
One clearly named person opens the note and records why the exception was made.
The message goes back to the last known handoff rather than being absorbed by any network member.
event.family_revolutionary_10_donor_dema: In the family parlor, a major donor puts a new envelope on the table and demands the next action target a rival's warehouse. The organizer replies that the building also stores food for the neighborhood.
You push the envelope back toward the donor; he stops speaking as if the money already bought the decision.
You circle the food stores on the plan; the organizer turns the sheet so the donor has to see them.
Your question forces the donor to explain why this specific rival matters so much to him.
Money Funds, It Does Not Command
The donor threatens to withdraw support if the cell refuses. Without his money, several safehouses lose supplies; with it, the cell risks becoming an instrument of private interest.
Refuse the target, keep dialogue open
The organizer refuses the warehouse but offers the donor a way to fund needs chosen collectively.
The envelope leaves with the donor; the network accepts a material loss rather than selling tactical authority.
The donor must choose: support the safehouses without dictating a target, or leave with his money.
event.family_revolutionary_10_mother_abs: The Message After Your Mother Leaves
A courier arrives with a note for your mother, but she is no longer present in the household. He wants to leave it with you 'because you know how the house works' and refuses to take it back.
You keep your hands behind your back; the courier remains holding the note and his unresolved problem.
You ask who replaced your mother; the courier realizes he was given no replacement contact.
You point to the box where your mother kept messages; nobody now has the key.
Her Absence Is Not Your Assignment
The network must recognize that a clandestine role does not automatically pass to a child when a parent disappears. The message can wait, change hands, or be returned.
The courier leaves to find the adult formally replacing your mother.
The sealed note goes back to the previous handoff instead of turning your home into an inherited station.
The note stays sealed in a neutral place until an identified adult retrieves it; you do not become its handler.
event.family_revolutionary_10_sabotage_a: Your father lays out a sabotage plan: cutting a bridge would stop a military convoy, but also the village's only medical cart. Your mother wants to delay; he fears losing the chance.
You mark the medical cart's route; your father has to look at it beside the convoy's path.
You remove the explosive marker; your mother keeps it in her palm while your father searches for another option.
Move the ambush past the bridge
You point to a stretch of road beyond the bridge; both parents recalculate the risk instead of arguing in principle.
Rejecting a Tactic Without Leaving the Cause
The operation still matters to the cell, but the bridge is not abstract. Your parents must decide whether they can slow the convoy without cutting the village's medical access.
The bridge stays intact; the operation becomes riskier for the cell but safer for civilians.
The operation is delayed and may lose its target, but nobody confuses urgency with a right to collateral harm.
Your parents keep the plan; they now explicitly accept that the military objective may cut a civilian service.
event.family_revolutionary_10_orphan_cal: After an argument about your housing, an organizer declares before the shelter: 'The Revolution is your family now.' A volunteer replies that a slogan decides neither who cares for you nor who comes for you at night.
You ask who will actually be there tonight; several adults stop nodding along with the slogan.
You reject the word; the volunteer asks everyone to speak in terms of concrete responsibilities.
You name specific people; the organizer can no longer replace their actions with the organization's name.
An Organization Can Help Without Declaring Itself Parent
The shelter must define who handles what: nights, care, school, evacuation. The movement can support you durably without claiming the word 'family' in return.
Each task gets a named person and backup; help becomes accountable rather than sentimental.
The organizer withdraws the phrase; nobody imposes an emotional bond to justify shelter.
You may call certain people close without turning the whole organization into a collective parent.
event.family_revolutionary_10_medicine_b: A crate of medicine reaches the neighborhood, but an organizer wants the first doses reserved for families already listed as sympathizers. The medic opens it anyway before a line containing several unknown families.
You move the political list aside; the medic puts her medical register in its place.
You help count the people waiting; the number already exceeds the available doses.
Your question pulls the discussion back toward symptoms rather than affiliation.
A Limited Crate, Not a Reward
There will not be enough medicine for everyone. The medic wants triage by medical need; the political organizer wants priority for people who helped the network.
Doses go to the most urgent cases, whether or not they ever helped the cell.
A small reserve remains for people exposed by an ongoing operation; the rest follows medical triage.
The political list takes priority over the medical register; aid clearly becomes a benefit tied to commitment.
event.family_revolutionary_10_recruiter_: The shelter separated its records, but a recruiter puts his chair directly behind the food line exit. People must pass him carrying their rations; he starts asking who 'wants to give something back.'
You drag the chair toward the back; the food line exit becomes clear again.
You open a side door; several families use it without passing the recruiter.
You repeat his phrase aloud; the cook immediately asks for the same explanation.
The recruiter says he forces nobody. The cook replies that a request placed between the ration and the exit is not neutral when people depend on the next meal.
People must choose to enter the recruitment room; nobody passes through it by necessity.
The shelter separates time as well: no political ask during relief distribution.
The table stays visible, away from the exit, with a sign stating relief depends on no answer.
event.family_revolutionary_10_minor_cour: After an adult courier is searched, a cell leader puts a small satchel before you and says Marines search children less often. He promises a short route to a nearby print shop.
You do not touch the satchel; the leader has to keep explaining the plan without implied consent.
You open the satchel with him; it holds wanted printing plates, not harmless letters.
Your question exposes the real calculation: the danger is exactly why the route is being offered to you.
Less Suspicious Is Not Less Endangered
The leader must choose between exploiting your low-suspicion profile and finding another route. You can support the objective without accepting selection precisely because you are a minor.
Give the satchel to an adult
An adult takes the longer route and carries the operational risk the cell wanted to shift onto you.
The satchel moves in stages without turning any child into a discreet courier.
Volunteer once with an exit plan
You accept this one route after setting fallback point, contents, and right to abort; nobody presents it as your new role.
event.family_revolutionary_10_civilian_t: A cell prepares to intimidate a foreman accused of informing the Marines. You recognize his name: the accusation comes from the same file where recruitment refusals had been treated as suspicious.
You put the old file beside the plan; the lack of evidence becomes visible before anyone leaves.
You cross out the address; the team leader can no longer pretend the visit is already settled.
Nobody in the room can name a direct witness; silence replaces certainty.
Some want to frighten him 'just in case.' Others point out a threat can create the enemy they only claimed to suspect. The cell must decide before the team leaves.
The team disperses; no threat turns a weak suspicion into real punishment.
Two people outside the original file must confirm a fact before any confrontation.
The team leaves despite the empty file; the tactic may protect the network, but knowingly creates risk for a civilian.
event.family_revolutionary_10_parent_or_: The Cell Takes the Family Kitchen
A cell meeting begins in the kitchen, the room your family had reserved for meals and rest. Your present parent objects; the organizer says urgency allows the exception without asking the household.
Clear the papers from the table
You stack the papers and clear the table; the organizer must physically take them back to continue the meeting.
You stand beside your parent; the objection can no longer be framed as one person's inconvenience.
You point to a room already meant for visitors; urgency loses its excuse for annexing the kitchen.
Backing Your Parent Is Not Leaving the Cause
The network needs a place immediately, but the home already has a discussed boundary. The cell must negotiate with the household instead of treating domestic refusal as disloyalty.
The cell changes rooms; the household rule survives precisely because it also applies during urgency.
Your parent agrees to one hour; the exception is explicit, limited, and does not become the new norm.
The meeting continues in the kitchen; your parent learns the household boundary can vanish whenever the organization declares urgency.
event.family_revolutionary_10_household_: An injured person reaches the family refuge and two adults already unroll the spare mattress in the common room. They promise 'only a few nights,' but nobody knows where residents will sleep if a second emergency comes.
You ask for a precise duration; the adults stop using 'a few' as a sufficient answer.
You move a chair to mark the area that must remain available to residents.
You look for blankets and a bench next door; the refuge gains an option without taking the entire common room.
The injured person must stay safe, but the household cannot expand forever. The adults finally set a duration, a replacement bed, and a plan if someone else arrives.
Another safehouse takes over on a written date; the shelter is real without becoming permanent by inertia.
One room remains outside the shelter operation even under network pressure.
The household opens one extra space for this emergency, with a clear boundary before the next one.
event.family_revolutionary_10_network_fa: The Exit Crossed Out in Pencil
An evacuation plan in the refuge shows three exits, but one was crossed out after a contact's arrest. Nobody has checked whether the second exit is still usable.
You follow the route to the yard; a stack of crates is in fact blocking the second door.
You ask why it is crossed out; nobody knows whether the danger still exists or the note was simply copied.
You count the residents; one door will not move everyone out quickly.
The Evacuation Plan Must Be Checked
The evacuation plan posted in the refuge decides who leaves by which door if Marines arrive. The cell must check the exits now instead of letting an old fear become an automatic instruction.
The crates are moved and the second exit becomes usable again.
An adult inspects the route before deciding whether it should remain forbidden.
The refuge replaces inherited notes with a plan verified that day.
event.family_revolutionary_13_money_with: After years of support, the adults managing the family's resources set aside money in your name before you turn fifteen. The same donor offers to increase it if you promise to defend 'his line' later.
You take the family envelope from the pile; the donor's conditioned money remains alone on the table.
You push both envelopes away; the donor loses his leverage and your family must decide what to do with its share.
You agree to keep useful introductions and addresses, but leave the tactical promise unsigned.
You are asked what you actually want to inherit: personal money, social access, or the freedom to leave without funding. Nothing should turn your future professional choice into debt to a donor.
Ten thousand Berrys are transferred clearly into your name, with no tactical claim and no political repayment.
You leave the money with the family and keep one explicit boundary: no donor can claim your future choice.
Keep access without a bought voice
You keep respectable introductions useful to the network, but access never becomes a vote on tactics.
event.family_revolutionary_13_mothers_un: The Post Your Mother Did Not Pass Down

The network finally shows you the clandestine post your mother held before her absence and offers training at fifteen. Her old handoff notebook stays closed on the table; nobody claims it belongs to you.
The organizer writes an invitation in your name instead of speaking of an inherited post.
You gently push the notebook away; the discussion stays on your future, not the role she left.
You refuse the specific post; nobody in the room can turn that refusal into a judgment on your mother.
The organizer accepts that the network must recruit you like anyone else. You may keep a bond with your mother, support the cause, or choose civilian life without those three answers being confused.
Agree to talk again at fifteen
Your name goes onto a future-invitation list, separate from your mother's post and without immediate commitment.
Choose civilian life without rejecting her
The network records that the family bond remains private; none of your mother's duties are transferred to you.
You accept the idea of future commitment for your own reasons, without claiming her notebook or post.
event.family_revolutionary_13_two_keys_t: Your parents put two keys before you: one opens a safehouse, the other the small family room they always kept outside the network. They ask what you want preserved before you turn fifteen.
You take the safehouse key; your mother leaves the family key on the table instead of taking it away.
You choose the family key; your father returns the safehouse key to the network without argument.
You bring the two keys together without mixing them; your parents understand you want both boundaries visible.
Cause and Home Are Not the Same Lock
Your parents ask for neither automatic loyalty nor rupture. They want a durable rule for what the network may open, what stays familial, and what you will decide yourself at fifteen.
You keep specific safehouse access, with a written rule that the family room is never included.
The network takes back its access; you keep a family space that requires no future career choice.
Two keys, two rules, and two responsibilities remain separate for your future.
event.family_revolutionary_13_invitation: The Invitation in Your Own Name
The shelter gives you a card bearing your name: at fifteen, you may ask to join a cell or simply use the lodging network while traveling. No box identifies you as a child of the organization.
You read the two separate lines; nobody can present lodging as political preregistration.
You fold the recruitment part under the card; lodging access remains valid on its own.
You keep the whole card; joining remains an option, not a substitute parent.
Shelter Does Not Create a Life Debt
The organizer confirms the card is neither a contract nor a family bond. It represents only two distinct doors you may open later—or never.
Your future access to safehouses is recognized without any obligation to become a revolutionary.
The network keeps an open invitation in your name for age fifteen, based on your choice rather than your lack of parents.
You decline both lodging and recruitment; the shelter closes your file without treating refusal as betrayal.
event.family_revolutionary_13_relief_wit: The medic gives you the small booklet used to track distributions in your neighborhood. It shows what your family received and helped redistribute, with no loyalty column or political debt.
You keep the booklet; the medic says it proves relief work, not membership.
You ask what remains of the small savings kept separate from distributions; the medic produces an envelope in your family's name.
Leave the booklet with the neighborhood
You leave the booklet with the next relief coordinator; your participation does not become personal property.
Scarcity never made your family virtuous. What remains is more concrete: knowing how to receive help without political debt, and give it without buying someone.
Five thousand Berrys in family savings are explicitly transferred for your first travels, with no political condition.
Carry the rule into the cause
You carry a network-recognized rule: future relief may never be claimed as recruitment debt.
You choose a future civilian life with one durable boundary: receiving aid creates no political obligation.
event.family_revolutionary_13_open_door_: The Open Door Without an Oath
The shelter finally puts up a simple sign: food and beds on one side, political volunteering in a separate room. You are asked whether you want to help maintain that separation when you are older.
You take a relief shift card; it carries no rank or oath.
You take the invitation from the second room; the organizer leaves the relief card separate on the table.
You take both papers without stapling them together; the separation stays visible even in your hands.
At thirteen, you are not joining any profession yet. The shelter can only leave you accesses and invitations you may choose to use from age fifteen onward.
You remain recognized as a future relief volunteer without enrollment in a political cell.
Your name receives an open invitation for age fifteen, separate from any aid received or given.
You may support relief and ask to join later without either becoming a condition for the other.
event.family_revolutionary_13_minor_cour: The cell leader returns the small satchel he once wanted you to carry. It is empty. He asks whether it should remain a future invitation symbol or proof that minors must never be default cover.
Hang the satchel on the wall
You hang the empty satchel on the wall; every new courier entering can see it.
You give the satchel back; the leader must decide what rule to keep without a commemorative object.
You keep the empty satchel at home; nobody puts a message inside or calls it your gear.
Your Age Must Not Be a Tactical Resource
The cell finally formalizes what this history established. You may still want to join later while refusing to let children be selected because they look less suspicious.
The cell records a durable limit: no minor is selected as courier merely to evade searches.
Keep the boundary outside the cell
You choose a future civilian path and keep proof that refusing one mission never meant refusing your own worth.
Your name stays on a future invitation, with a written condition that you may still refuse each mission.
event.family_revolutionary_13_tactic_wit: The File Closed, Not the Cause

The once-suspected foreman comes to testify: nobody had recruited, threatened, or seen him inform. The cell removes his name from the file and asks what this mistake changes in your relationship to the cause.
You close the empty file; the foreman stays in the room to hear what comes next.
You ask who will acknowledge the error; the organizer stops calling it mere 'caution.'
Say the tactic is not the cause
You separate the failed tactic from the political goal; several members agree without asking you to forget the harm.
The cell can apologize, revise its rules, or minimize the affair. Your inheritance need not be a choice between blind loyalty and total rupture.
Stay close with an evidence rule
The network adopts independent verification before intimidation; you keep the option to join at fifteen.
You choose a future civilian path while keeping ties with people willing to repair their mistakes.
The foreman receives a public apology and your future invitation remains open without requiring you to forgive everything.
event.family_revolutionary_13_parent_not: The Kitchen Returned to the Household

The cell formally returns the kitchen to the household as non-operational space. Your present parent asks whether this family victory changes what you want at fifteen; nobody from the network is invited to answer for you.
Keep the rule on the door
You leave the rule posted; your parent knows you protect the home without necessarily rejecting the network.
Ask to act outside the home
You ask whether future involvement could begin elsewhere; the kitchen stays outside the operation.
You state a future civilian preference; your parent treats it as neither family abandonment nor political betrayal.
Your Parent Is Not the Organization
Your relationship can survive your future career choice. The household boundary becomes concrete inheritance: no cell may invoke your parent to automatically claim family space.
Keep the cause outside the home
You keep a future invitation to join elsewhere while the home remains explicitly outside the operational network.
Stay civilian and close to your parent
The family relationship strengthens without becoming an argument for or against a revolutionary career.
Join later without conflating the bond
You consider joining at fifteen for your own reasons, with a written rule always separating parent, home, and cell.
event.family_revolutionary_13_protected_: The Witness Who Keeps His Name
A civilian agrees to publicly correct a false accusation by the cell, but only if his address enters no political file. Some want to keep his details 'just in case' after he testifies.
You return the address card to the witness; the cell loses the copy it might have kept by habit.
You separate his words from his contact details; the file can prove the error without storing his private life.
Ask how to contact him later
You ask him directly; he chooses an intermediary rather than his home.
Protecting Someone After Using Their Evidence
The testimony helps the cell repair a wrong, but grants no permanent right over the witness. They must decide what remains after the meeting.
The network keeps only an intermediary chosen by the witness and bans political reuse of his address.
You choose a future civilian path and the cell destroys its copies after receiving the testimony it needed.
The witness chooses a relay for possible verification; that permission remains limited to this case.
event.family_revolutionary_13_household_: The Rule Written on the Door
Before you turn fifteen, the household writes on the back of the door what the cell must ask before using a room, a piece of furniture, or a family member. You are left to add the final line.
You add the phrase; the adults reread the whole rule from the start.
You write that an emergency needs an owner and an end point; the organizer signs below.
You add the final line; no clandestine family role can now be presented as your natural inheritance.
The door may stay behind, but the rule can survive into your future choices. You must decide whether it travels with a revolutionary invitation or a civilian life.
Carry the rule into the cause
The network recognizes the household boundary as a condition of any future involvement from you.
Keep the rule for civilian life
You keep the boundary without any promise to join; the family is no longer an implicit organizational reserve.
Keep an invitation without inherited role
Your name remains invited at fifteen, but no parental role, room, or family resource is automatically included.
event.family_revolutionary_13_network_fa: The Name on the Safehouse Map
The network shows you a safehouse map with names crossed out and replaced over the years. You are offered a simple recognition code for future help, without being given any cell role.
You memorize the code and the map is closed; you take no list of addresses.
Ask if the code requires joining
You ask before accepting; the organizer clearly separates relief access from recruitment.
You decline future access; the organizer removes your name from the distribution list without political comment.
A Network Can Be a Resource, Not a Destiny
The code can offer shelter in the future. By itself, it says nothing about the career you will choose at fifteen; that decision remains separate.
Keep the code as a civilian
You keep emergency access to the network without an active political invitation.
Beside the relief code, your name receives a separate invitation to discuss joining at fifteen.
You leave with neither code nor invitation; the network does not turn your refusal into family or political debt.
event.family_royal_01_mothers_glove.text: The usher calls your mother before the petitioners. She is still crouched to fix your shoe; he holds out her glove and reminds her the whole court is waiting.
event.family_royal_01_mothers_glove.choi: You refuse to release her sleeve; the usher stops looking at the clock.
You push the glove toward her. Your mother smiles before standing.
You stare at the man hurrying your mother. He finally looks down at you.
event.family_royal_01_mothers_glove_i01_: Your Mother Hesitates Before the Audience
Before the audience doors, your mother still holds your glove. The usher waits for the ceremony cue; she can leave, delay the opening for you, or ask him to change the planned order.
She stays one second longer, enough for protocol to yield to your bond.
You let her go. Before you have words for it, you understand that her role can interrupt yours.
The glove falls. Your mother picks it up herself, and the usher understands you are not part of the ceremony's furniture.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.title: Two Places Behind You
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.text: For your first official portrait, servants line your parents up behind your chair. Your father makes you laugh; a master of ceremonies orders him one step back to preserve the order of titles.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.choice.r: You reach for him and immediately ruin the planned pose.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.choice.t: You turn toward your mother. The painter asks everyone to start again.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats.choice.g: You grab the cloth behind you. Two servants catch it before it falls.
event.family_royal_01_two_seats_i01_reac: The painter waits. Your father finds the order absurd; your mother points out the servants will be blamed if the sitting collapses. Both look to you before taking their places.
Your parents step closer despite the floor marks. The painter will have to work with your actual family.
You stay still. The portrait will be perfect, and you already learn that perfection assigns everyone a precise place.
You refuse to turn; they come to you instead. The master of ceremonies swallows his correction.
event.family_royal_01_empty_nursery.text: Before the wardship council visits, a steward takes a small family miniature from your nursery and boxes it away. “The register is not settled yet,” he mutters.
event.family_royal_01_empty_nursery.choi: You catch the corner of the box before it leaves the table.
You push his hand away. The steward stops, surprised that such a small child already refuses.
You let the box go, but not the key that locks the cabinet.
event.family_royal_01_empty_nursery_i01_: The steward hesitates: leaving the portrait recognizes a family history the council wants to control; hiding it means deciding what your own room is allowed to say.
The miniature stays. The council will see it, even if it dislikes what it implies.
The box closes. You remember where the steward puts things people do not want you to see.
Your finger returns to the pale rectangle on the wall. The steward realizes absence is visible too.
event.family_royal_01_fishman_balcony_ba: Before a balcony appearance, an adviser slides your water basin behind a curtain: he wants the crowd to see “a royal child first.” Your skin is already starting to dry.
You reach toward the curtain until the adviser understands what you want.
You hit the railing hard enough to interrupt the preparations.
You turn away from the light and refuse the position prepared for you.
The adviser proposes wetting a cloth discreetly out of sight. A servant waits with the basin while the balcony doors are already opening.
The basin remains visible beside you. The court will have to present your body as openly as your title.
You get relief without the crowd seeing how. Comfort and image have already been split apart.
The appearance begins without you. The adviser will have to explain why his perfect image lost its subject.
event.family_royal_01_giant_archway.text: Your ceremonial canopy will not fit under the arch with your giant cradle. A household officer orders the bearers up the service stairs rather than move the decorations.
event.family_royal_01_giant_archway.choi: You push the cloth above you; a ribbon drops at the officer's feet.
You reach toward one of the bearers who is already struggling for breath.
Your cry drowns out the orders. The whole procession stops on the stairs.
event.family_royal_01_giant_archway_i01_: The bearers can force the service route, or the officer can finally remove two garlands from the main arch. The cost of convenience is not yours alone.
The garlands come down. For once, the palace changes instead of making the people carrying you bend.
The procession goes around the back. You will grow up knowing who pays when the décor refuses to move.
They carry you another way and the canopy goes on empty. The ceremony survives, but not exactly as planned.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.title: The Velvet Hood
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.text: For an official minute of silence, a dresser presses a heavy velvet hood over your Mink ears. It slips at once; the master of ceremonies blames the dresser for cutting it badly.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.choice.p: You yank the velvet off and drop it on the carpet.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.choice.t: You catch the dresser's hand as he is being blamed.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood.choice.h: You hold the hood down yourself until your ears protest.
event.family_royal_01_mink_hood_i01_reac: The dresser offers to cut two openings on the spot. The master of ceremonies refuses: uniformity matters more than a garment that can actually be worn, and the servant may keep the blame.
Hand over the hood to cut
Two openings are enough. The silence starts late, but no one can pretend your body was the mistake.
You remain bareheaded. The master of ceremonies keeps his rule; you refuse to wear its flaw.
You endure the hood until the signal. The dresser avoids punishment, but you remember the price of silence.
event.family_royal_01_thin_silver.title: One Silver Plate
event.family_royal_01_thin_silver.text: An important visitor arrives. The steward puts the household's last silver plate before you and hides the servants' mended bowls. Your title is expected to look richer than the house.
event.family_royal_01_thin_silver.choice: Push the plate to the edge
You push the silver toward the edge of the table, toward the bowls being hidden.
You turn the fine plate into a drum. The visitor looks over.
Your hand leaves the silver to trace the crack in a mended bowl.
event.family_royal_01_thin_silver_i01_re: The steward wants the scene restored before the visitor enters. Behind him, a cook waits with the bowls she was told to make disappear.
The bowls remain in sight. The household looks less wealthy and much more real.
The silver returns to you. You learn that a title can demand hiding scarcity instead of solving it.
Hand the plate to the cook
The steward has to retrieve the plate from the cook in full view of the visitor.
event.family_royal_01_seal_ribbon.title: The Registry Ribbon
event.family_royal_01_seal_ribbon.text: A clerk ties a ribbon bearing the family seal around your wrist before entering you in the public register. He warns the nurse: if you tear it, she will answer for the delay.
event.family_royal_01_seal_ribbon.choice: You immediately tug at the knot. The nurse catches your wrist without daring to grip hard.
You rub the seal between your fingers until wax marks your skin.
You hold your wrist out to the clerk as if the gesture already belonged to you.
event.family_royal_01_seal_ribbon_i01_re: The register opens to your name. The nurse watches the ribbon more than you, because a royal child's smallest mistake can become an ordinary adult's fault.
You stop pulling. The nurse finally breathes, though no one asked you to understand why.
The ribbon tears. The clerk sighs, but this time the nurse says plainly that it was not her fault.
Give the ribbon to the nurse
You put the seal in her hand. For one second, the family symbol belongs to the person carrying the risk.
Your mother has just come to read to you when a minister opens the door without waiting: three petitioners are already in the antechamber. “Your presence is required now.”
You hold out the open book. The minister remains in the doorway, file in hand.
You slip after her before anyone can send you back.
You push the door against the minister. Your mother suppresses a laugh before reopening it.
event.family_royal_04_mother_keeps_door_: Five Minutes That Belong to Someone
Your mother can delay the hearing, take you with her, or go alone. The minister points out that the petitioners travelled for two days; your story can wait.
You sit at the back of the antechamber. Duty stops being only the thing that takes your mother away.
Your mother closes the file for exactly five minutes. The minister waits, and you learn that time can be negotiated.
You keep the book. She keeps the hearing. Neither of you pretends the two duties cost the same.
event.family_royal_04_parents_two_lesson: Your father teaches you to greet the old guard by name. Your mother arrives with the master of ceremonies: in ten minutes you must receive an ambassador using the exact formal greeting.
You repeat the guard's name loudly under the master of ceremonies' stare.
You repeat your mother's formula word for word. Your father raises his hands in surrender.
You combine the ambassador's title with the guard's familiar tone. Your parents look at each other.
What a Greeting Says About You
Your parents are not arguing about manners, but what manners should protect: the useful distance of office, or real relationships with the people who live around you.
Your father helps you remember faces. Your mother agrees, provided you also learn what each title requires.
You repeat it until you no longer hesitate. Your father stops joking when he sees what the effort costs you.
They finally have to explain their disagreement instead of using you as a practice field.
event.family_royal_04_wardship_keys.text: You find the family miniature box in a wardship-office cabinet. The key hangs from a sleeping clerk's ring; on the next shelf, several letters bear your name.
event.family_royal_04_wardship_keys.choi: You lift the small key without waking the clerk.
You tug his sleeve and point to your name on the letters.
You leave the key where it is and compare the seals on the envelopes.
event.family_royal_04_wardship_keys_i01_: The clerk wakes. He says the council reads all mail to a royal child first “for your protection.” He does not say who protects you from the council.
He hands you one after recording the incident. You gain one page and discover the administrative cost of a simple request.
You return the key, but now you know the cabinet, the ledger, and the exact rule separating you from your mail.
You recover the miniature without touching the letters. You choose which boundary to cross.
event.family_royal_04_fishman_proof.text: A minister places your small chair beside the fountain for visiting dignitaries. You hear him say your presence “proves the kingdom welcomes every people.” Nobody asked you to be that proof.
event.family_royal_04_fishman_proof.choi: You drag your chair out of the planned position, inch by inch.
Your question cuts off the minister before the visitors arrive.
You leave the chair and sit beside the servant holding the damp towels.
