event.family_royal_04_fishman_proof_i01_: The minister simplifies: “It is a good image.” A palace worker looks away. Even at four, you understand that a good image can require someone to stay quiet.
The minister has no concrete answer. For the first time, his staging produces a question he cannot control.
You stay, but answer in your own words. The image slips out of his control without disappearing.
You leave before the visitors arrive. The minister keeps his speech and loses the living proof he wanted at its center.
event.family_royal_04_giant_servant_step: Every reception morning, four servants drag a heavy platform into the hall because the royal furniture is too small for you. Today one of them traps his hand under a step.
You lift one corner of the platform long enough to free his hand.
You shout for them to stop. The bearers freeze the platform in the doorway.
You stay on the floor when they ask you to climb onto the platform.
The household officer proposes continuing: “Only one reception left.” The injured servant holds his hand while everyone decides whether palace convenience is worth the strain.
The reception moves to an empty gallery. It is less impressive, but nobody has to carry the décor on your behalf.
You help move it. The servants save time; you learn that sharing a burden does not automatically make the burden fair.
You receive the visitors standing. The palace discovers that a rule can survive without its official furniture.
The ceremonial hood has been replaced with an open collar, but the wardrobe master summons the tailor: the alteration was never authorized. He wants someone held responsible.
You stand against the tailor's leg before he can apologize.
You bring back the old hood and put it between the adults.
You repeat the word they keep using until the wardrobe master turns to you.
event.family_royal_04_mink_tailor_blame_: The tailor says he altered the garment because you could not wear it otherwise. The wardrobe master says he should have asked permission from people who never had to wear it.
The blame moves to you, where it suddenly loses much of its force. The tailor keeps his post.
A few seconds make the problem visible. The rule can no longer hide behind ignorance.
The tailor agrees to follow procedure. You gain an official route, but it is still controlled by people who do not bear the garment.
event.family_royal_04_creditor_bows.text: A creditor bows deeply to you, then orders his men to take two cooking pots from the kitchen. The steward mutters that the royal branch will pay “when appearances improve.”
event.family_royal_04_creditor_bows.choi: You plant yourself in the doorway as the men reach for the pots.
You ask why he bows if he can still empty the kitchen.
You bring out the silver plate the steward saves for visitors.
event.family_royal_04_creditor_bows_i01_: The creditor refuses the plate: it is worth less than the debt, but far more to appearances. The cook waits to learn whether she must make dinner without pots.
You refuse to let the debt fall straight onto the kitchen. The steward will have to find another payment.
The steward pales, but the creditor agrees to revisit the account. The title loses some of its display before the staff lose their tools.
The pots leave under a perfect bow. You do not forget that respect can coexist perfectly with injustice.
During a public festival, a guard stretches a rope to keep the crowd away from the royal table. A child on the other side stares at the decorative loaf before you; nobody is meant to eat it.
You lift the loaf with both hands. The guard immediately understands where you mean to go.
You call the child over. The guard blocks the very first step.
Ask the guard to give it
You push the loaf toward the guard and ask him to pass it across.
event.family_royal_04_bread_beyond_rope_: The guard explains that breaking the line in public could cost him his post. The loaf will be thrown away after the ceremony if nobody changes the rule.
You cross the rope yourself. The guard did not disobey; the crowd still saw who was allowed to cross.
You leave the loaf where it is to protect the guard. Waste becomes the visible price of the rule.
You force the master of ceremonies to answer in front of the crowd. He permits the sharing rather than explain the refusal.
event.family_royal_04_household_fallback: A bell rings in the corridor and the whole staff changes pace: your toys vanish, curtains are straightened, voices drop. An official visitor is approaching your rooms.
You slip your toy behind a cushion before a servant can take it.
You keep playing as if the bell has nothing to do with your room.
You pick things up with the staff, not fully understanding why the urgency exists.
The visitor is not coming to see you live; he is coming to see how a royal child lives. The difference is enough to transform your room and everyone's work.
The visitor finds a real room instead of a set. The staff hold their breath, then discover the world does not end.
You cross a room that suddenly feels less like yours. You learn what image requires without anyone explaining it.
Ask the staff what they prefer
The staff choose what actually needs tidying. For once, preparation stops being a cascade of orders.
event.family_royal_04_court_fallback.tit: The Chair You Must Not Touch
event.family_royal_04_court_fallback.tex: In a small waiting room, a clerk forbids you from sitting in an empty chair: it belongs to someone higher in precedence, even though that person did not come.
event.family_royal_04_court_fallback.cho: You sit in the empty chair. The clerk opens his mouth, then looks at the door.
You sit on the carpet directly in front of the reserved chair.
You ask the name of the absent person who still owns the seat.
event.family_royal_04_court_fallback_i01: The Chair Reserved for Someone Absent

In the waiting room, the clerk recites the rule: the empty chair belongs to someone of higher rank, even while absent. Nobody is offended, but everyone must arrange their body around that forbidden seat.
You push the chair to the wall. The clerk may restore it later; for a few minutes, absence stops commanding the room.
The clerk explains the full order. You learn that a court can turn almost any room into a ranking.
You refuse to choose between the floor and an empty rule. The corridor becomes your temporary seat.
event.family_royal_07_petitions_under_do: After seeing you at a hearing, townspeople slide three petitions under your door instead of using the official office. A clerk is already coming to take them back before you read them.
You pick up the first sheet before the clerk reaches the door.
Block the door with your foot
You wedge your foot in the door and keep the petitions behind you.
You call for your mother loudly enough that the clerk stops in the corridor.
A Hearing That Followed You Home
The clerk says answering directly would set a precedent. The three pages describe a broken well, a market tax, and a brutal guard; the problems already exist.
You have each name entered in the ledger instead of letting the pages vanish. Procedure takes the complaints in without erasing them.
You return the pages after reading them. The office keeps control of the file, but not of what you know.
An hour later, the three residents enter through the official door. You have turned a shortcut into a public obligation.
event.family_royal_07_parents_on_steps.t: Before a ceremony, your father goes down to personally greet an injured guard. Your mother stays above: if she follows, the procession is officially late. If she does not, he faces the master of ceremonies alone.
event.family_royal_07_parents_on_steps.c: You go down the steps toward the guard and your father, in front of the whole procession.
You stay beside your mother while the master of ceremonies counts the seconds.
You call the guard up to you. He looks at his bandaged leg, then at the stairs.
event.family_royal_07_parents_on_steps_i: The guard insists nobody should change the program for him. Your father replies that a rule demanding his discretion after an injury mainly protects everyone else's comfort.
The procession waits. Your mother eventually comes down too, turning the delay into a family decision rather than one person's offense.
The ceremony leaves on time. Your father stays below for a few minutes and joins later, without pretending you all made the same choice.
The guard does not have to climb the steps: the first official greeting happens where he can stand.
event.family_royal_07_council_signs_for_: An angry merchant produces a notice bearing the family seal: the wardship council raised her stall fees “in the name of the royal house.” You had never seen the decree.
You take the notice and read your own name in the closing formula.
You ask which council member chose the increase. The clerk first answers with the institution's name.
You ask the merchant what the increase costs her rather than what the decree claims to raise.
The council explains that a royal minor cannot decide, but the royal name guarantees continuity. The merchant answers that continuity does not pay for her market stall.
The next notice will also name the responsible councillor. Your seal at least stops fully erasing the actual author.
The council accepts a limited review. You do not erase the rule, but you refuse to let your name make debate impossible.
The decree stands. You now know that not deciding does not stop your name from producing consequences.
event.family_royal_07_fishman_harbor_que: During a harbor visit, Fish-Man workers ask why they still have to use a separate entrance to the royal docks. Your escort hands you the prepared answer: “security reasons.”
You begin the written sentence. The workers wait without interrupting.
Ask the guard for the reason
You turn to the guard and ask what security reason actually requires that gate.
Ask how long it has been
You ask how long the separate entrance has existed. Several hands rise at once.

On the dock, the escort talks about cargo control. The workers show the separate gate they must use, while the same crates pass elsewhere without a detour. Your question is less convenient than your official face.
You walk the detour with the workers. The rule stops being a sentence and becomes extra time, distance, and inspections.
You give the prepared answer. The visit continues neatly, but nobody on the dock mistakes your presence for change.
You promise only to raise the question, not to solve what you do not yet control. The escort writes down every word.
event.family_royal_07_bell_for_crowd.tex: For the palace festival, you are asked to lift a great bell before the crowd “because everyone will be impressed.” Two workers are still holding a badly fixed brace under your platform.
event.family_royal_07_bell_for_crowd.cho: You ignore the bell and crouch to see what the workers are holding.
You take the bell; the crowd roars before it fully leaves its cradle.
You fold your arms in front of the bell. The presenter holds his smile one second too long.
event.family_royal_07_bell_for_crowd_i01: The organizer wants to use the crowd's excitement. The workers warn that the brace is shifting. Everyone knows you can lift the bell; the real question is what others must risk to prove it.
The crowd waits while the brace is reinforced. When the bell finally rises, nobody is underneath holding it together.
You pull off the show. The workers do too, but nobody applauds them for keeping the danger out of frame.
You refuse to be the only spectacle. The workers come onto the platform and explain what they had to reinforce.
event.family_royal_07_tailor_before_cour: The tailor presents a new design that fits your Mink ears while keeping the house colors. A councillor wants to approve it only for you, so other servants cannot use it to request adaptations.
You ask why the alteration should be royal when the clothing problem is not.
You ask the tailor to show the other designs he prepared.
You accept having the garment approved only for you.
The councillor calls it a personal favor. The tailor replies that a cut preventing pain and discomfort is craft knowledge, not a reward for rank.
The council authorizes an adaptable pattern for service uniforms. Your privilege becomes a precedent others can use.
You get a comfortable outfit. The tailor puts away the other patterns, and you see exactly where privilege stops.
You refuse to be the only person the rule knows how to accommodate. The council must reopen the issue or return to the old problem.
event.family_royal_07_full_procession_em: The Procession and the Empty Purse
The treasurer says your household must fund its place in the royal festival despite its debts. In the corridor, you hear two employees discussing wages delayed again to pay for the procession horses.
You ask why horses come before wages. The treasurer half-closes his ledger.
You tell the two employees you heard them. Neither knows whether to apologize.
You announce you will not take the carriage to the festival. The treasurer immediately calculates the difference.
The treasurer warns that a royal branch disappearing from ceremonies loses political weight, which may cost even more later. The staff, however, need their wages this week.
You attend with fewer horses and less display. The rank remains visible without consuming everything it claims to represent.
The procession is flawless. Wages wait again, and now you know who really finances perfection.
The household misses part of the festival. The staff receive what they are owed before the title receives its display.
event.family_royal_07_apology_written.te: After a public incident, the palace gives you an apology to copy. It admits to “an unfortunate misunderstanding” without naming the guard, servant, or resident who actually paid for the scene.
event.family_royal_07_apology_written.ch: You strike the word from the polished draft. The clerk presses his lips together.
You refuse to begin until you know who the apology is actually for.
You copy the formula unchanged. The text becomes neat, official, and almost empty of people.
event.family_royal_07_apology_written_i0: The clerk explains that naming a specific fault could bind the house. A vague apology protects the image; a precise one could force someone important to repair something.
Your apology becomes more dangerous because it becomes verifiable. It can now be accepted, challenged, or used to demand repair.
The wording protects the house from any clear obligation. You learn how a polite sentence can close a door.
You refuse to make paper do all the work. The harmed person can at least answer someone who carries the palace name.
event.family_royal_07_household_fallback: Dinner is served an hour early because an unexpected meeting will take the room later. The staff rushed the whole kitchen; you are not hungry and nobody wants the food wasted.
You sit and start eating because everyone already worked for this time.
You ask to save your plate for later. The cook looks toward the coming meeting.
You suggest someone else eat what was prepared if you cannot finish it.
The meeting never asked the kitchen whether the hour worked. The kitchen never asked whether you were hungry. The decision came from above and everyone only passed it downward.
The meeting moves. For once, powerful people's schedule adapts to work already done.
You eat without hunger and the room clears on time. You see how a small burden becomes invisible when everyone complies.
Food no longer needed for protocol goes to the staff on duty. Nothing is fixed, but nothing is wasted.
event.family_royal_07_court_fallback.tex: You wait for a ceremony on a side bench. Two officials discuss a family removed from royal housing in front of you; they speak as if you are too young to understand the word “eviction.”
event.family_royal_07_court_fallback.cho: You repeat the word. The two officials immediately stop speaking as though the bench were empty.
You keep your eyes elsewhere and let them finish the sentence.
You ask where the family will sleep now. Neither file contains that answer.
event.family_royal_07_court_fallback_i01: The officials can explain the unpaid rent, the rule, and the signature. They are much less certain about what happens after the housing door is taken back.
The file gets an extra note: check rehousing. It is not a solution, but it is no longer an administrative ending.
The rule is clear, and so is the consequence. You learn that a decision can be perfectly proper and still humanly incomplete.
You memorize the name before the file closes. Administration has a number; you keep a person.
event.family_royal_10_future_alliance_li: Your mother finds your name in a file of “future alliances”: several houses already suggest a later engagement. The adviser insists this is not a marriage arrangement, merely keeping doors open.
You take the file before the adviser closes it and read the names beside yours.
You ask your mother what she thinks of the list rather than what the adviser expects.
Ask what you are useful for
You ask what exactly your presence in that column is meant to gain for the house.
The adviser talks about ports, votes, and future treaties. Your mother says your existence is not a pending diplomatic promise. He asks whether she really wants to close options for the kingdom.
Your name leaves the list. Any future alliance will have to begin with a real decision, not your childhood silence.
The file stays open but no house receives an answer. You keep the information without turning it into commitment.
You agree only to revisit it later. The adviser gets a door left ajar; your mother makes sure he writes nothing more.
event.family_royal_10_succession_chart.t: A succession chart is unrolled before the council. Your name is nowhere near the top: it appears several branches down, surrounded by notes about what happens if other heirs die or renounce.
event.family_royal_10_succession_chart.c: You count the people ahead of you in line. The clerk waits for you to reach your own name.
You ask who decides the scenarios written around living members of your family.
You fold away the section containing your name. The rest of the succession remains visible.
event.family_royal_10_succession_chart_i: The adviser says nobody is preparing you for the throne; he is preparing the institution for every possibility. Yet that caution already shapes what they teach you and where they want you kept.
You learn the obligations without pretending the throne is meant for you. Knowledge becomes preparation, not prophecy.
Refuse a life built around the chart
You reject schedule changes justified only by hypothetical accidents. The council keeps its chart, not your timetable.
Ask what is required of everyone else
The discussion finally leaves your single box and reveals a whole family organized around possibilities no child chose.
event.family_royal_10_public_reform_with: After repeated complaints about access to the docks, the palace prepares a poster announcing “a harbor for everyone.” The main entrance will open more widely, but some separate controls remain. Your portrait is meant to prove the house is already moving forward.
You cross out “for everyone” on the poster. The printer stops before starting the run.
You ask when the study ends. The adviser searches for the line that does not exist.
You refuse to let your face go to print with a change that has not happened yet.
The Poster Promises Before the Reform

The minister shows the poster where your royal name announces a port for everyone. Tomorrow, however, the affected workers must still use the separate entrance. The campaign sells an intention before any rule truly changes.
Condition your portrait on a real measure
Printing is suspended until a first dated measure is signed. Your image stops being free advance payment for the palace.
The poster mentions the review and the still-separate entrance. The message becomes less polished and much harder to misuse.
The posters go out. You learn how much faster a symbol can move than the people it claims to represent.
event.family_royal_10_staff_pays_scandal: After your earlier incident, the palace reassigned two servants and suspended a guard “to restore discipline.” Your public apology mentioned none of it; you learn by accident.
You ask to see the decisions made after your apology. The clerk realizes you already know about the penalties.
You leave the official corridor to find the people whose punishment appears in no speech.
Ask why the public record is silent
You compare the posted apology with the internal sanctions. The two documents tell different stories.
An Image Repaired With Other Lives
The palace explains that staff are responsible for royal appearances running smoothly. Nobody says you asked for these penalties; that did not stop them being imposed to protect your image.
Several penalties are reversed. You cannot erase the past humiliation, but you refuse to leave it as the price of your image.
An addendum to the apology acknowledges that your own choices caused the incident. The court loses part of its protective screen.
The penalties stand. You now understand that your privilege can operate even when you never ask it to.
event.family_royal_10_procession_invoice: The treasurer opens the old file on your house's fall: a decree seized land after a political crisis, but older debts also bear the family seal. A letter from your great-uncle calls all of it “theft.”
You line up the decree, the debts, and the letter. Some debts predate the seizure; other losses really did come from the punishment.
The treasurer separates property taken by decree from assets handed over to creditors.
You trace the accounts back to a loan signed before the political punishment. The fall does not have a single cause.
Two Truths in the Same Ledger
Neither story is enough alone: the house suffered a real political seizure, but it was already in debt. The family letter merges both into a fall caused entirely by enemies.
You ask which current debts can be settled without recreating the old grandeur.
You draw two columns: what was genuinely seized and what the family already owed.
You keep the letter as the main story. The decree was real; the debts become easier to forget.
event.family_royal_10_subjects_at_gate.t: A protest forms at the palace gate after a new local tax. The council asks you to cross the courtyard in full view to show the house “hears the concern,” without announcing any measure.
event.family_royal_10_subjects_at_gate.c: You go beyond the planned mark and get close enough to hear full sentences.
You refuse to appear until someone can tell you what the palace will do after your walk.
You stay in the corridor. The councillors lose the silhouette they wanted in the windows.
event.family_royal_10_subjects_at_gate_i: Behind the gate, protesters demand a hearing and numbers. The council wanted an image of listening; the crowd now asks what happens after someone actually hears.
A small delegation comes in with its accounts. The problem remains, but the gate stops being the palace's only answer.
You have the demands recorded with names and numbers. Your role becomes a conduit rather than decoration.
You cross the courtyard and go back inside. The crowd saw you; it still has no answer about the tax.
event.family_royal_10_guard_refuses_orde: A dignitary orders a guard to remove an old vendor from the royal route. The guard hesitates: she has a market permit, but her stall “spoils the view” of the procession.
You stand beside the guard instead of moving on with the procession.
You ask to see the vendor's permit. It carries the market seal.
You ask which rule allows the stall to be removed. The dignitary first answers, “propriety.”
The guard can obey the dignitary and contradict the permit, or respect the permit and risk discipline for insubordination. Your name is enough to change which risk looks more serious.
The guard leaves the stall and records that you backed his reading of the permit. The dignitary can no longer call it simple disobedience.
The vendor accepts a nearby spot and compensation. The procession gets its view without making her bear the whole cost of propriety.
The stall disappears before the procession. The guard obeys, the vendor loses her day, and the street looks perfectly orderly.
event.family_royal_10_household_fallback: A clerk brings three documents for your household to countersign. Your place is already marked at the end of the table even though your signature has no legal force yet: they want you to learn the gesture.
You ask for the pages before the pen. The clerk hands you the first document.
You fill the practice sheet with your name without touching the official documents.
Ask why your seat is ready
You ask why they are training the gesture when it still decides nothing.
The clerk says training starts early so you will not hesitate when it matters. He has no equivalent lesson prepared on the right not to sign.
Learn the gesture and the reasons
You practice the signature, but only after reading each page. The habit forms with a question attached.
You learn to write your name without letting practice blur into obedience to the documents in front of you.
The pen stays clean. The clerk notes that the first thing you learned about signing was that you could refuse.
event.family_royal_10_court_fallback.tex: An empty seat now bears your name in certain meetings even when you do not attend. Today an official piles files on it because he knows you are still too young to come.
event.family_royal_10_court_fallback.cho: You sit down in front of the pile. The official has to retrieve his files one by one.
You open the file placed on your name because nobody expected you to come.
You move your nameplate to the far end of the table where nobody prepared a chair.
event.family_royal_10_court_fallback_i01: The council chair says your seat is mostly symbolic for now. Yet the symbol already creates the impression that your branch is represented in decisions you never hear.
You stay for one file and leave before a symbolic seat becomes fictional attendance.
The council agrees your nameplate appears only when you are actually present. Absence stops counting as decorative assent.
Your seat remains in meetings. You learn that representation can exist long before participation.
event.family_royal_13_open_court_name.ti: Your Name Before the Open Hall
event.family_royal_13_open_court_name.te: For the first time, you are offered the opening words at a public hearing in your own name. The prepared text promises only “attention and continuity”; beyond the doors wait the same kinds of petitions you have seen before.
event.family_royal_13_open_court_name.ch: You take the sheet and read its three lines before the doors open.
You ask to see the files before deciding what to promise the people who wrote them.
You step down before the announcement. The master of ceremonies must choose someone else.
event.family_royal_13_open_court_name_i0: The hall waits. You hold neither throne nor profession at thirteen, but your name already opens a door many petitioners cannot push themselves.
Use the name to open access
You open the hearing without pretending to govern. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; inherited access remains a tool, not a royal career.
You state your limits clearly. The hall gets fewer promises and more truth; At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian.
You refuse the podium without rejecting the petitioners. At fifteen, your Active entry will remain civilian; family duty does not automatically become a profession.
event.family_royal_13_family_not_institu: Your mother waits alone after one last meeting about your future. She tells you she can remain your mother even if you refuse the obligations the court wants attached to your name. The council expects your answer tomorrow.
You sit beside her without speaking. For once, nobody takes notes.
You ask what she would choose if her public role had no claim on you.
You ask the question no file contains: will she stay if you step away from court?
She does not promise it will be simple. She promises only not to turn affection into a signature. Tomorrow, the council may lose an obligation without you necessarily losing your family.
Keep the bond, leave the obligation
You keep your bond with your mother without keeping a court obligation. That boundary becomes a lasting part of your inheritance.
You accept a limited set of family obligations. At fifteen your career stays civilian, but that duty can still open future situations.
You ask for distance. A personal 5,000-Berry fund makes that autonomy concrete without erasing the family bond.
event.family_royal_13_seal_without_thron: The Seal Without a Promise of a Throne
The council gives you a copy of the family seal for your personal records. It announces no rank or succession: only proof that you belong to this history, whatever place you choose next.
You take the seal without asking anyone to unroll the succession chart again.
Ask what it does not grant
You first ask what this seal does not allow you to decide.
You leave the seal where the council placed it. Nobody makes you take it.
The clerk lists its limits: no professional authority, no new title, no automatic right over other people's lives. It still carries memory and access.
Carry the history, not the power
You keep the seal in the family archive as proof of origin, not professional authority.
Use the name only to open doors
You accept archive access without pretending it makes you right. That privilege remains usable and contestable.
You leave the seal with the council. Your origin remains true, but no physical symbol becomes necessary to prove it.
event.family_royal_13_symbol_or_voice.te: At thirteen, the palace is already preparing a new campaign about partial dock reform. Some restrictions will remain. They ask for your portrait and voice before the measure can speak entirely through its results.
event.family_royal_13_symbol_or_voice.ch: You read the exceptions before looking at the poster mock-up.
You refuse the photo session until affected dockworkers are in the room.
You push the portrait away without denying that the partial opening is a real improvement.
event.family_royal_13_symbol_or_voice_i0: The measure genuinely improves access without ending every separation. You can support the step, criticize it, or refuse to become living proof of it. Your royal origin does not make your voice palace property.
Support the progress and name its limits
You speak, but the campaign also names what remains unresolved. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; your voice no longer belongs automatically to palace messaging.
Your portrait moves behind those living under the rule. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; your reputation already reflects that choice.
You refuse the campaign without rejecting the reform. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; your voice will not automatically serve as institutional proof.
event.family_royal_13_pay_the_cost.title: What Is Owed to You
event.family_royal_13_pay_the_cost.text: At thirteen, the treasurer gives you copies of the decree, the debts, and the family letter. The court asks what you still consider “owed” to your branch before another adult writes the answer for you.
event.family_royal_13_pay_the_cost.choic: You mark only the land and property the decree actually took from the family.
You cross out acknowledged debts and set lost old privileges apart from the rest.
You close the file before the word “owed” becomes a personal obligation.
event.family_royal_13_pay_the_cost_i01_r: The file gives no single answer: some seizures are documented, some debts are real, and some privileges were never rights. You must decide what you want to carry forward from the fall.
You renounce the old claims. A cleanly liquidated 10,000 Berrys becomes a fund to rebuild without recreating former grandeur.
The court recognizes a documented share of the seizure. 25,000 Berrys are restored without erasing debts the family genuinely owed.
You keep the names and the claim open. Your reputation now carries a demand you may pursue later.
You abandon restoration. 5,000 Berrys from the last liquid assets become a fresh start instead of a payment toward the past.
Keep the name, not the claim
You keep the name without turning former comfort into a debt the world owes you. That stance becomes publicly recognizable.
event.family_royal_13_walk_beyond_gate.t: The palace is already preparing a series of supervised civilian visits for when you turn fifteen, all chosen by the household. The gate is open; a clerk wants to know whether you accept that future program or will chart your own route.
event.family_royal_13_walk_beyond_gate.c: You read the visits one by one: safe markets, allied institutions, not a single day left open.
You tear the sheet through the first month. The clerk does not move.
You keep one visit that interests you and return the rest of the schedule.
event.family_royal_13_walk_beyond_gate_i: Nobody offers you a royal career: there is none. The real question is how much control the court keeps over your civilian life simply because it can open doors for you.
You pass through the gate without an official itinerary, wearing unmarked travel boots. Your origin stays real without becoming your schedule.
You keep a few useful visits and reject the rest. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian, with inherited access you will use case by case.
You accept a heavily supervised civilian start without mistaking it for a career. Distance from court will have to be negotiated later.
event.family_royal_13_household_fallback: A steward returns the key to your childhood rooms: the palace is already reassigning some spaces ahead of your fifteenth birthday. You must decide what the key still means to your family.
You close your hand around it. It opens a room, not a profession.
You place the key in the steward's palm. The room will remain, but not as an obligation.
Ask who will use the room
You ask what happens to the room and the work around it when you no longer live there.
A House That Remains Behind You
The steward reminds you that your name will always get you received here. You can accept that refuge, leave it behind, or treat it as a relationship rather than an automatic right.
You keep the key as family access. The old hound that slept outside your room leaves with you; returning remains a choice.
You return the key and ask to be invited like any relative. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian, with concrete distance from court.
Ask that the room serve another use
You suggest the empty room serve visitors or staff on duty. At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian; an old privilege becomes at least a usable space.
event.family_royal_13_court_fallback.tit: The Last Place in the Register
event.family_royal_13_court_fallback.tex: The family register opens a line reserved for “orientation at fifteen.” The clerk cannot enter any professional royal rank: he can only ask what relationship you want to keep with the family institution.
event.family_royal_13_court_fallback.cho: You write the only professional status that actually matches this departure.
You leave the space blank rather than invent a title the world does not recognize.
You add that royal affiliation remains family origin, not a profession.
event.family_royal_13_court_fallback_i01: The clerk accepts the distinction: your family remains `royal_family`, but your Active entry will be civilian. Later Events may let you choose a personal affiliation without rewriting your origin.
At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian without cutting every family obligation. The inheritance remains pressure and access, not a career.
At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian and ask the court to stop scheduling your life. The name stays in your history, not your calendar.
At fifteen, you will enter Active as a civilian with one rule: if your name opens a door, also look at who remains outside.
event.active_sabaody_red_line_passage.te: At Sabaody, the ship is coated for the descent beneath the Red Line. The deep current leads toward Fish-Man Island.
event.active_sabaody_red_line_passage.ou: The coating holds through the pressure and current. Fish-Man Island appears in the depths.
event.active_new_world_route_start_raiji: At Fish-Man Island, one New World needle locks onto Raijin Island. The bearing promises violent weather.
You rise beyond the Red Line and take the stormbound course toward Raijin Island.
event.active_new_world_route_start_risky: At Fish-Man Island, one New World needle fixes on Risky Red Island. The current is rough, but the course is clear.
You rise beyond the Red Line and enter the New World on the course toward Risky Red Island.
event.active_new_world_route_start_mysto: At Fish-Man Island, one New World needle settles on Mystoria Island. A deep current offers a clean line forward.
You rise beyond the Red Line and follow the current toward Mystoria Island.
ui.departure.grandLineOutcome: You leave the Blue behind and take the current toward Reverse Mountain.
event.active_generic_sea_01_baited_distr: They laugh at your bluff and throw their hooks knowing you are alone.
Two fake castaways contradict each other and the ambush collapses before it starts.
Your story does not hold; they close in to verify it.
Their leader hesitates long enough to reveal the hidden boat.
Claim an imaginary escort
You spot the trap just as a hook already bites into your rail.
You spot the second boat hidden behind their sail before it can emerge.
You hesitate one second too long; their skiff presses against your side.
The wounds are painted and a grappling line is hidden under the tarp.
Read their setup
They stop playing injured and show their teeth.
Show them you do not believe it
You keep enough sea between you to force their game into the open.
Give them a wide berth
Two sailors smeared with fake blood wave a white cloth from an intact skiff. Their sail hides something low on the water just behind them.
The Too-Clean Wreck
You turn too late and their bow strikes your side.
You make them cross their own line and force them to let go.
You shake them loose, but the impact tears away a plank.
Your turn leaves their hooks pulling at empty water.
Break their boarding angle
A line tightens around your arm and slams you into the rail.
You throw a hook back into their rigging and jam their attack.
You cut one, but a second still holds the hulls together.
The hooks come free before their crew can haul on them.
Cut the grappling hooks
They grab the money and lose enough time for you to break contact.
Throw them a small purse
The skiff drops its tarp. Three grappling hooks whistle toward your rail as a second boat bursts from behind the sail.
The Hooks Come Out
You chase them just far enough to make clear they are not coming back.
Drive them off
The two boats disappear before a second fight can begin.
Let them run
You send them off with a clear warning instead of a pointless chase.
Give them one warning
Their leader spits out the name of a busy passage before breaking away.
Trade their escape for information
Their boats pull away but stay close enough to shout. Their leader wavers between fleeing, bargaining for an exit, and one last provocation.
Within Shouting Distance
event.active_generic_sea_01_barrel_survi: The barrel rolls under you and you slam hard into the rail.
You lift him with the barrel and lay him flat on deck.
You get him aboard, but he swallows more water before reaching the deck.
You pull him from the water before his hands give out.
Haul him up before he slips
The rescue goes badly and the castaway reaches deck barely breathing.
The medic anticipates every move and has him on his feet almost at once.
The medic stabilizes him, but he is too weak to speak at once.
The medic organizes the rescue and the castaway quickly comes around.
Let the medic direct the rescue
The castaway grabs it. You pull him aboard without taking a special risk.
Throw a line and slow down
A lone sailor clings to an overturned barrel. His former ship is still visible on the horizon, but it never slows and nobody turns back for him.
The Man on the Barrel
You give him a temporary place aboard and he finally settles.
Keep him aboard until a port
You let him recover before deciding anything.
Let him breathe before questions
He admits striking his officer after weeks of unpaid wages.
Demand his story first
The ship refuses to turn back. The silence confirms part of his story.
Signal his old ship
Barely recovered, the sailor says his captain threw him overboard after a pay dispute. The other ship keeps sailing away without answering.
The Abandoned Hand
You simply answer that you have seen them without pretending to understand the message.
They answer with an enthusiastic salute, convinced you know their local code.
You identify an old merchant convention used to ask for news without hailing.
You realize they are mainly asking whether the route behind you is safe.
A distant ship repeats three flags that match no common code. It is clearly waiting for an answer, but does not change heading.
event.active_generic_sea_01_contested_fl: You signal for them to take it and continue without a fight.
Let them have the chest
The hook misses and swings back into your rail.
You lift the chest before their line even hits the water.
Both hooks catch together and jam the chest between the ships.
Your hook catches first and pulls the chest to your side.
Hook the chest first
Your offer sounds weak and the other crew demands everything.
You get a clear agreement and even a witness on each deck.
They refuse the split and throw their hook at the same time as you.
Their captain agrees to split before the lines cross.
Offer a split before hooking it
A salvage chest floats between your ship and another schooner. Both crews nearly throw their hooks at the same moment and freeze.
One Chest, Two Hooks
You leave with more, under curses from the other deck.
Claim the larger share
Your nerve is enough to make them soften part of their claim.
Claim the chest was already yours
The chest holds enough Berrys for both sides to leave satisfied.
Split it evenly
You leave them the money and keep only the satisfaction of avoiding escalation.
Give them the contents
The chest opens on several dry purses. The other captain is already counting coins aloud and watching both your hands.
The Lid Comes Off
event.active_generic_sea_01_crossing_wak: You open so much distance they can no longer force their wake on you.
Break off the crossing entirely
You refuse to be pushed off course. The ships pass far too close.
Hold your line
You raise a sharp signal before their stern has even passed.
Signal their mistake
You take their wake from a distance and avoid contact.
Give way early
A large galleon crosses your heading without slowing and forces you to take its wake broadside. Its crew watches as if yielding were obvious.
The Forced Wake
Their officer bows, admits the fault, and returns to his ship.
Accept their apology
After arguing, the officer pays a small sum to avoid a feud between captains.
Demand compensation
You refuse to waste more time and signal them away.
End it
The officer leaves annoyed, but both crews laugh at the exchange.
Throw their arrogance back at them
Minutes later, a launch leaves the galleon. An officer comes to offer very polite apologies, but only after seeing your reaction.
The Apology Launch
event.active_generic_sea_01_deck_challen: The plank rolls under your foot and you fall hard against your own hull.
You turn at the end of their yard and return to offended silence.
You get back aboard soaked under their laughter.
You cross the plank and return before they finish counting.
Take their plank wager
You throw their challenge back as a joke and both ships move on.
Decline with a laugh
You overplay it and their captain raises the stake against you.
They end up betting against their own champion.
They smell the bluff and keep the upper hand in the negotiation.
You turn their challenge into an almost even wager.
Turn the wager around with words
A loud crew holds speed a few meters away. They push a plank over the water and bet nobody on your ship dares cross it.
The Plank Between Decks
Their captain quietly removes the sailor who had been pinning the plank with his foot.
Call out their cheating
The noise starts again and both decks begin betting on everything.
Accept their second wager
You refuse to prove anything more and resume your heading.
Let them have the last word
You pocket what you are owed and refuse to let the game become a feud.
Take the result and leave
Their captain refuses to let it end simply. He pulls out a second purse and offers to double the wager while his men already start cheating.
One More Wager
event.active_generic_sea_01_distress_lan: They confirm they can talk, but cannot steer their ship.
Answer the signal from a distance
The swell throws the hulls together; your planking takes the hit.
You slide into their dead angle and stop their drift cleanly.
You come in too fast and scrape their hull before stabilizing.
You place your ship within reach without creating a second problem.
Come alongside cleanly
The lanterns shrink behind you.
Keep your course
Even your navigator misreads their drift; the hulls collide.
Your navigator catches them in a pocket of calm water and stops the drift.
The approach stays safe, but costs planking and time.
Your navigator settles both ships side by side.
Let the navigator choose the approach
A merchant brig drifts broadside. Three red lanterns blink from its stern while the crew waves a hawser: its rudder no longer answers.
Three Red Lanterns
You help them brace the rudder long enough to resume their route.
Talk them through a temporary repair
You cut it short before their breakdown becomes your problem.
Leave them to manage
The captain hands over a purse before you pass the hawser.
Negotiate before towing
You take their weight on your line. Their captain promises to remember the gesture.
Take them in tow
Their rudder chain snapped clean through. The captain asks for a tow until they can brace the tiller and continue alone.
The Broken Rudder
event.active_generic_sea_01_drifting_mai: You protect the bag until you can return it without reading a single name.
You spot a coastal courier farther on and return the bag still sealed.
Keep it sealed and signal it
One envelope is enough to identify the mail service that lost the bag.
Read one letter to find an owner
You find a few Berrys tucked into an envelope and keep them.
A tarred mailbag floats intact between two currents. Several envelopes stick out of the closure, but the postal seal still holds.
event.active_generic_sea_01_empty_deck.c: A sheet line snaps under your weight and slams your shoulder.
You immediately see someone left the deck in a hurry, but not overboard.
You board without immediately seeing what is wrong.
You spot fresh tracks and a cabin locked from the outside.
Nobody answers, but three dull knocks come from below their deck.
You refuse to feed your crew to a mystery that asks for nothing.
A loose line gives way during the inspection and damages your own planking.
Your shipwright spots a hatch locked from the deck before you even board.
The vessel looks sound, but the silence remains unexplained.
Your shipwright confirms nobody abandoned this vessel long ago.
Let the shipwright read the vessel
event.active_generic_sea_01_empty_deck.t: A small sailboat keeps almost your speed, sails trimmed and table set, but nobody is visible on deck. A cup still steams beside the tiller.
event.active_generic_sea_01_empty_deck_i: The lock gives and several voices speak at once beneath your feet.
Open the hatch
You step back, but the pounding below deck becomes frantic.
Return to your ship at once
You shift the wrong crate and a tool drops onto your head.
You find the key and fresh prints leading from the deck to a missing boat.
You find nothing more before the knocking starts again.
You find the key hidden beneath a mooring bitt.
Search before opening
Three dull knocks finally answer your calls. The main hatch is locked from the outside, and one key is missing from the ring by the tiller.
Three Knocks Below Deck
Their quartermaster locked everyone below, took the payroll, and fled in the boat.
Question them before leaving
The captain gathers a small sum rather than argue while his ship drifts.
Claim a reward
You let them out and return their ship. Their relief is immediate.
Free the sailors
You simply return the key and let their crew take control again.
Ask for nothing
The hatch opens on a furious captain and several sailors locked below for hours. Their quartermaster vanished with their boat and payroll.
The Locked Crew
Your crew improvises an even more ridiculous flag and the other deck bursts out laughing.
You answer without a real threat, strongly enough that they remember your flag.
Their joke dies on its own without an audience.
Their captain finally lowers the mocking flag without a word.
Stare them down until they lower it
A passing crew raises a crudely painted flag caricaturing your ship. They are clearly waiting to see whether you laugh, get angry, or answer.
event.active_generic_sea_01_fresh_wrecka: You go around the field and leave the pieces behind.
Go around the debris
You follow the wrong line and a timber hits your hull.
You trace the drift almost immediately to an overturned hull.
You circle for too long before finding the trail again.
The debris draws a clear line toward something heavier.
Read the debris drift
You lean too far and hit the rigging while catching your balance.
You spot two people under an overturned hull before they can even shout.
You see nothing until a dull knock sounds from beneath an overturned hull.
A hand briefly appears beneath an overturned hull in the distance.
Search for survivors
Split planks, a boot, and a torn piece of sail pass your hull. The wood is not waterlogged: the wreck happened very recently.
Fresh Wreckage
You guide them from outside until they find the opening themselves.
Keep them talking
The hull drops on you and crushes your hand before being pushed away.
You roll the hull over in one effort and both survivors finally breathe open air.
You lift it enough for one survivor to escape, but the other stays trapped a moment longer.
You make enough room to get both survivors out.
Lift the overturned hull
You use your rigging to gradually free both people.
Rig lines under the hull
Two people breathe in an air pocket beneath a small overturned boat. The hull sinks lower with each wave and the space is shrinking.
Under the Overturned Hull
The heat forces you too close and your rigging catches theirs.
You stop their drift while keeping your sails beyond the flames.
You get close, but a spark burns your planking before you pull away.
You place your ship exactly where the smoke spares you.
You keep your sails intact and shout instructions from your deck.
The rope burns through your grip and you slam onto their deck.
You cross before the flame reaches the yard and clear the way for others.
You make it across, but burn yourself landing near the galley.
You land behind the smoke, close enough to help immediately.
A nearby schooner pours black smoke from its ports. The fire has left the galley and climbs toward the mainmast while the crew panics.
event.active_generic_sea_01_galley_fire_: The chest slips and crushes you against the bulkhead before being shoved away.
You clear both the chest and the burning partition in one effort.
You free it, but the heat burns your arms.
You get the chest overboard before the flames reach it.
You turn their panic into organized movement and limit the injuries.
You sacrifice part of their cargo to smother the main fire.
Someone shouts that their powder store sits behind the already-hot partition. Flames have reached the door, but not the chest yet.
The captain gathers a purse and insists that you take it.
The cook admits leaving an open lamp beside an oil cask.
You leave them their money and depart with their gratitude.
The fire is finally contained. The soot-covered captain looks over the blackened deck, then turns to you with a purse and many questions.
event.active_generic_sea_01_inspection_s: The officer catches the inconsistency immediately and brings his cutter closer.
The officer salutes and nearly apologizes for stopping you.
Your story convinces nobody; they demand to board.
Your story holds well enough to turn the inspection into a verbal check.
Invent passage orders
You reduce speed and their officer moves to routine questions.
Accept the inspection
You cross their bow too closely and tear away a piece of planking.
You position so cleanly that their officer gives up the show of force.
You keep the distance, but with a hard maneuver that strains the ship.
You hold exactly the distance they request.
Hold regulation distance
A government cutter raises the inspection flag and cuts across your heading. Its officer asks identity, origin, and reason for travel without accusing anyone yet.
The Inspection Flag
They find nothing worth stopping the voyage over and return to their boat.
Let them inspect the deck
The officer admits they are looking for a ship of another color and shortens the inspection.
Ask for the exact grounds
A few minutes of tea are enough to lower the tension between both decks.
Turn the inspection into conversation
You accept the questions but not their boots on your deck. They carefully note your flag.
Refuse boarding
The verbal check ends, but the officer now asks to see your deck and hold. He claims to be searching for a reported ship in the area.
The Search Request
event.active_generic_sea_01_medicine_fla: The captain pays before accepting your help.
You wish them luck and keep your distance.
Your medic crosses over with a kit and the fever soon stops climbing.
You show them how to cool the patient and stay until he breathes easier.
A schooner raises the sickness flag and asks for help. Their cook has burned with fever for two days, and nobody aboard knows what to do.
The patient describes the flags and currents seen over the last few days.
He gives enough detail to recognize several silhouettes from far away.
You end the conversation and give them the quiet they need.
The fever drops enough for the cook to speak. He insists on returning the favor before the ships part.
event.active_generic_sea_01_overboard_de: He grabs you at the wrong moment and both of you slam into the hull.
You haul him aboard and open distance before the other ship completes its turn.
You haul him up, but his old ship has already turned toward you.
You get him on deck before the other captain can react.
Pull him aboard before they turn back
Your questions make him panic and he swallows water before answering.
You get his story and the names of two witnesses before even hauling him up.
He shouts too fast to be clear while the other ship turns back.
He explains a wage dispute clearly enough for you to understand the stakes.
Make him explain from the water
You give him something to hold while both captains close in to talk.
Throw him a float without taking him aboard
You hold your heading and leave their dispute behind.
Stay out of it
A sailor suddenly jumps from a nearby cargo ship and swims toward you. His captain turns at once and orders you to send him back without explanation.
The Sailor Who Jumps
Under both crews’ eyes, the captain finally hands over part of the unpaid wages.
Demand his wages be paid in front of you
You refuse to decide for him. The sailor chooses not to return to his old ship.
Let him choose for himself
The other captain pays quickly to get his man back and end the scene.
Return him for payment
You place the sailor under temporary protection. The other captain notes your flag before leaving.
Refuse to send him back
The sailor accuses his captain of withholding months of wages. The other ship immediately offers a purse if you return him without argument.
The Withheld Wages
event.active_generic_sea_01_powder_barre: The first shot sets off two barrels together and the shock hits your hull.
Your gunner sets off the whole line in a chain well ahead of your bow.
The shot clears a path, but throws splinters onto your deck.
Your gunner pops the barrels one by one at a safe distance.
Have the gunner shoot them from range
You clip a barrel that bursts against your hull in a sharp detonation.
You use their drift to pass without ever exposing your broadside.
You get through, but a nearby blast tears splinters from your planking.
You find a safe line through the barrels.
Thread the gap between barrels
You let the line of barrels drift ahead until a gap opens.
Reduce sail and wait
A line of tarred barrels drifts across your route. A short fuse sticks from one and still smokes: someone dumped them recently.
The Tarred Barrels
The captain pays to know exactly where the trapped line lies.
Sell the warning
The captain describes a small raider trying to close off their route for two days.
Ask who is after them
You signal only the immediate danger and resume your heading.
Stay out of the rest
The merchant changes course immediately and thanks you for warning about the charges.
Warn the merchant
A merchant ship appears behind the line of barrels and heads straight toward it. Its captain clearly has not understood what is floating ahead.
The Merchant Behind You
event.active_generic_sea_01_sealed_crate: The hook snaps back and cuts your forearm before the crate bangs into the hull.
You catch it in one motion and set it dry on deck.
The crate bangs your planking before you finally haul it aboard.
You recover it cleanly without losing your heading.
Hook the crate as you pass
The crate disappears in your wake without costing you a minute.
Leave it drifting
You keep it in sight. A cutter soon appears and heads straight for it.
Mark it and wait
A copper-banded crate floats just below the surface, too clean to come from an old wreck. A merchant mark has been scraped off its lid.
The Banded Crate
After a few curses, the captain pays to recover the cargo.
Claim a salvage fee
The captain stares at you for a long moment, then leaves without proof.
Deny seeing it
The lid reveals ordinary navigation instruments. The mystery dies immediately.
Open it before returning it
The cutter takes back its crate and thanks you for avoiding an incident.
Return it without fuss
A cutter slices toward you. Its captain recognizes the crate immediately and demands it back, without explaining why its mark was scraped away.
The Owner Arrives
event.active_generic_sea_01_signal_barte: Your curiosity eventually pulls out details they had not planned to share.
You quickly learn which ports they avoid and which they seek.
The sloop stops signaling and moves off without particular resentment.
Each crew leaves with two or three useful names and one more dubious story.
A sloop matches your heading and raises a string of merchant flags. It offers port and ship news in exchange for your own rumors.
event.active_generic_sea_01_song_across_: Your deck finds the rhythm and both crews trade the same chorus until they part.
Your verse draws laughter, then an even cheekier answer.
Invent a verse to provoke them
The deck becomes percussion and even the quietest crew members join in.
You let their song carry over the water for a few minutes before the wind takes it.
A fishing ship crosses your heading singing loud enough to cover the sails. As you pass, its crew throws the chorus at you like a challenge.
You show them how to raise enough canvas to move under their own power.
You refuse to tie your ship to their problem and continue.
They accept the price and pass over their hawser.
You pass a line and accept losing some speed for them.
A small cargo ship has lost its mainmast and barely moves under a jury sail. Its captain asks for a tow until it can continue alone.
event.active_generic_sea_01_tow_request_: They open a sack: only rope and spare parts, badly redistributed after the break.
They complain, then pay to use your deck as temporary storage.
You tolerate a few sacks as long as they keep the passage clear.
You block the way and the sacks go back to their deck.
Make them take the sacks back
As soon as the towline tightens, their sailors start placing sacks on your deck without asking. Their captain claims he is only balancing his boat.
